# Norn — Build Log

One line per sub-checkpoint. A checkpoint is ✅ only when its "done when" is fully
true, the suite is green, and it is committed. Gates in `PLAN.md` are ticked only
when every line of the gate is true.

Method (binding): TDD (red → green → refactor), one package = one responsibility,
dependencies point inward (`cmd/` → `internal/*` → stdlib/crypto), interfaces at
boundaries only, no package imports a sibling it doesn't need. The **Python
reference implementation** under `contrib/norn-ref/` is written *from the spec,
first*, and generates the vectors the Go code must match — so the Go code never
becomes its own oracle.

## Phase 1 — Core library (Go)

Decision after 0.13b: start Phase 1 rather than run a fifth gate. Phase 1 *is* a
second implementation of §4 and §5, so it surfaces spec gaps as a side effect of
being useful, and `PLAN.md` already schedules a cold-model gate at Phase 6
against the frozen spec.

Rule for this phase: the Go code is written **from `SPEC.md`**, and the vectors
are the oracle. Where Go and the Python reference disagree, the spec decides —
and if the spec is silent, that is a defect to record, not a coin to flip.

| # | Checkpoint | Done when | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | `internal/cbor` | deterministic encoder + strict decoder; every encoding negative rejected, every valid entry round-trips byte-exact | ✅ |
| 1.2 | `internal/entry` | envelope, `kid`, preimage, sign/verify, entry and leaf hashes; all 16 entry mirrors reproduced | ✅ |
| 1.3 | `internal/cjson`, `internal/state` | canonical JSON + state schema; every JSON file in the suite round-trips byte-exact | ✅ |
| 1.4 | `internal/replay` | every `(index, reason)` in the manifest, `state.json` byte-exact, and all 12 `genesis/` aborts | ✅ |
| 1.5 | `internal/note`, `internal/trust` | receipt verifies; fingerprint reproduced; all 14 `trust-bad/` rejected | ✅ |
| 1.6 | Fuzzing | 83.8M executions across three targets, zero failures | ✅ |
| 1.7 | Cross-implementation check | entries rebuilt in Go from their semantic values, signed independently, bytes identical to the shipped vectors | ✅ |

### Decision resolved — 0.6 was approved and run (2026-09-19)

0.6 requires giving a **fresh model** only `SPEC.md` + `testdata/vectors/` and
having it implement an entry verifier that passes every vector. That means
spawning a subagent, which I do not do without an explicit go-ahead.

Why it matters *now* rather than later: I wrote the spec **and** the Python
reference, and I am about to write the Go implementation from the same spec.
All three share my blind spots. A genuinely cold reader is the only thing that
proves the spec is self-sufficient — and a spec gap is far cheaper to fix before
the Go code exists than after.

| Option | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Run it now** (recommended) | One subagent run; spec gaps found before Phase 1 |
| Defer to Phase 6 | Plan already has a cold-model gate on the frozen spec; Phase 1 will surface *some* gaps, but only the ones I happen not to share |
| Skip entirely | `SPEC.md` never independently validated; the "second implementation" claim in `PUBLICATION.md` §7 weakens |

Loop paused here pending that answer.

- **2026-09-19 · 0.7c Tier-3 closed** — the eight remaining questions the gate found answerable two ways by the prose **and** unexercised by the vectors are now decided in `SPEC.md` and pinned by vectors 42–48 (log is 49 entries). Seven of the eight already matched the reference implementation — they were simply never *stated*, which is the failure mode the gate exists to catch. The eighth was a real change:
  - **D-032 · proof of possession on `rotate`**: a rotate that installs a new identity key must now be signed by **both** the current and the incoming key. Only the device can rotate, so installing a key it does not hold harms only itself — but irrecoverably: it could never rotate again without a signer-assisted re-enrolment. It holds both keys at that moment, so the second signature costs nothing, and it matches D-008 for `enroll`. Four tests, vectors 40 (accepted) and 46 (rejected).
  - **D-033 · `bad-thr` vs `root-invariant`**: `bad-thr` is about the *value* being outside `1 … len(set)`; `root-invariant` is reserved for a `root_remove` shrinking the set below the threshold. Both previously fired on `root_thr` with `thr > len(roots)`.
  - Also stated and vectored: unauthorised `revoke` → `threshold` (43); `role` outside the enum → `decode`, now explicitly distinguished from a well-formed signature whose `kid` does not resolve (44); `sigs` mandatory, omitted → `decode`, empty → `threshold` (45); and the per-type check order proved by entries wrong in two ways at once — 47 (device signature before `dup-id`) and 48 (root quorum before the per-type rule).

## Phase 2 — The log + CLI

The first phase with external dependencies. Ground rule 3 of `PLAN.md` is the
constraint that matters here: **reuse the transparency ecosystem, do not fork
it.** If an unmodified `transparency-dev/witness` cannot cosign a Norn
checkpoint, the design is wrong — so that is a gate line, not an aspiration.

What this package adds is the part x/mod does *not* implement — the C2SP path layout, since x/mod uses the sumdb scheme instead.
  - The chunked path encoding is the classic interop bug in this format: `N` is written as 3-digit groups with `x` on every group but the last, so 1,234,067 is `x001/x234/067`. Tested at 0, 1, 255, 1000, 1234, 1234067, and with partial widths — wrong paths here look plausible and resolve to nothing.
  - `ParseCheckpoint` refuses anything but the three canonical lines: no trailing-newline omission, no empty origin, no leading zeroes or `+` in the size (Go's `ParseInt` accepts `+42` quite happily), no non-32-byte root, and **no extension lines**, which §6 forbids.

Norn's graph is **3**, and Norn's pitch is that it runs on a NAS and a Pi. **D-049** records the trade honestly — including the strongest argument *for* Tessera, that the dependency would land only in `norn-log` and never in `nornd` — and fixes a falsifiable upgrade trigger: adopt it when the log outgrows one directory, needs a second writer, or needs a cloud backend. Ground rule 3 is untouched, because it is about *formats* interoperating, and 2.6 tests that directly.
  - The store writes the layout, recovers from it, and serves it. Entry bundles are the authoritative record; tiles and the checkpoint are derived, so a torn write to either repairs itself. **The checkpoint is written last**, so a crash leaves a log whose advertised size is behind what is on disk, never ahead — the reverse would advertise entries a reader cannot fetch.
  - **Two real bugs, both caught by tests written first.** The partial-bundle path was built by asking for width 0, which produced `…000.p/0.p/*` — a plausible-looking path that matches nothing. And each append wrote a *new* partial file (`.p/1`, `.p/2`, …) while leaving its predecessors, so a reader globbing the directory found several with no rule for choosing, and picked the narrowest. **That is the orphan-file hazard again** — the one that left seven stale vectors in the suite and survived three conformance runs. Partials are now superseded rather than accumulated, with a test asserting no `.tmp` file survives a clean run.
  - Go: 14 packages, 80 tests, graph still **3 modules**.
- **2026-09-19 · 2.4 + 2.5 `internal/logclient` — the verifier loop, end to end.** Taken together because the verifier and its *refusals* are one idea: a verifier that reproduces the right state but accepts a tampered log has not verified anything.
  - **The headline test**: the fixture's own 91 entries are written into a real served tile directory, read back through the same `Fetcher` a node will use, and the state that comes out is **`state.json` byte for byte**. Until now replay was handed a list of entries; this is the first time they arrive the way they actually will — as bundles on a disk somebody else controls. §10 now has a real path through it.
  - **Order matters, and the code says why**: integrity is checked **before** replay. The served entries are rebuilt into a tree and required to hash to the head the checkpoint advertises; only then are they replayed. Replaying first and checking afterwards would mean acting on entries never shown to belong to the log — exactly the trust a transparency log exists to remove.
  - Four refusals, each a different lie a log operator can tell: a **forged head** (root replaced), a **tampered entry** (one byte flipped inside a bundle), a **missing bundle** (advertising entries it cannot serve), and a **wrong anchor** (which must abort with `bad-genesis` and yield no devices, never a populated state built on a genesis the anchor does not pin). Plus a restart that must change neither checkpoint nor state.
  - `Fetcher` is deliberately **one method wide**. Everything a verifier needs from a log is "give me the bytes at this path" — and keeping it that narrow is what will make peer gossip (`GOSSIP.md`) a different `Fetcher` rather than a second verifier.
  - Go: 15 packages, 86 tests, graph still 3 modules.
- **2026-09-19 · 2.6a — the ecosystem reads a Norn checkpoint unchanged.** Checkpoints are now signed notes, with the key name equal to the origin: the same binding §9.1 requires of the trust file's log key, so a checkpoint signed by a key named for another network cannot verify here even if that key is trusted elsewhere. `transparency-dev/formats/log` — the package witnesses actually use — parses ours and reads back the same origin, size and root; it rejects a wrong key, rejects an **origin mismatch** (a valid signature for a different log is still the wrong log), and rejects a checkpoint whose size line was altered. Our own verifier agrees with it in both directions.
  - **Cost, measured as before:** `formats` is **6 modules**; the full witness binary is **80**. The graph went 3 → 7. The witness's extra 73 are its HTTP handler and storage, which are the witness's business; what is Norn's business is whether the bytes are right, and that is what this proves.
  - **2.6 is explicitly NOT closed.** The gate says an unmodified witness *cosigns* a Norn checkpoint, and a cosignature round trip needs a witness **process** answering `add-checkpoint`. That is a lab item, and `GOSSIP.md` already places witness deployment in Phase 4. Marking 2.6 done on the format half would be exactly the partial credit this build log exists to refuse — so it is split: **2.6a ✅, 2.6b ⬜ Phase 4**, and the `PLAN.md` gate line says the same.
  - Go: 15 packages, 91 tests.

Claiming that compatibility is exactly the unverified assertion §7 carried until 2.1 tested it.

Refusals tested for a swapped entry (genuine proof, genuine checkpoint, wrong entry — the substitution the bundle exists to catch), a foreign checkpoint, a tampered proof hash, and the wrong log key.

  - **§12 now states that the suite has two provenances.** Entry, state and trust vectors come from the Python reference and Go must match them; `served/` and `proofs/` come from Go, because producing a tiled log requires an implementation. Now each half is checked against **its own** generator: the reference half via `gen_vectors.py`, the Go half via `make vectors-log`. A check that cannot express the structure it guards is not a check.

Reading the same log from disk and over HTTP must give the same state and the same checkpoint, and does. The fetcher bounds every response (a verifier fetches from a log it does not trust, so answering a request must not be enough to exhaust it) and refuses a path that escapes the log root **before sending it** — a verifier should not ask, and a proxy might honour it.

It refuses without `-trust`, refuses an anchor that fails §9.1 validation, and refuses an unreachable log rather than reporting an empty network as healthy. The summary prints what was **rejected** as well as what was accepted: a tool that shows only the good news is the wrong shape for this job.

Checkpoint **0.13b** gave genesis a non-default `mmd`, which changed the genesis entry, which changed `genesis_hash`, which lives in the trust file, so the fingerprint moved and the worked example silently became fiction. Exactly the D-045 failure, in the one place my citation test did not look. Fixed, and `internal/specdoc` now checks the fingerprint example too — **a worked example nobody verifies is worse than none, because a reader trusts it.**

  - **What the format had to decide.** One `sig`, not §4.1's `sigs` array, because a request carries exactly one signature and the key that made it is *in the object* — there is no `kid` to resolve and no threshold to count. A preimage prefix that differs from §4.2's, so a device signature over a request can never be replayed as a signature over an entry; both implementations assert that directly rather than trusting the prose.
  - **And what it must not claim.** `ENROLLMENT.md` said `norn sign` means "a request that doesn't own its WG key is never even displayed". That is false: `wg_pk` is X25519 and §3 says it never signs, so the signature proves possession of the *device* key only. Fixed in both documents, with the bounded consequence spelled out (`dup-wg` catches a live key; an unheld key denies service to its own requester). **The same class as the §7 claim that stood unverified until 2.1** — a sentence that sounds like a guarantee and is not one.
  - **bech32m (D-050)**, HRP `norn`, checked against **BIP-350's own published vectors** in both implementations, plus **BIP-173's valid bech32 strings, which must all fail** — the two differ only in the checksum constant. The one rule Norn drops, the 90-character limit, is asserted *narrowly*: that single string must decode while every other invalid vector still fails, so the deviation cannot quietly widen. A negative vector re-encodes a real request under bech32's constant, so "we reject bech32" is tested with the same bytes rather than a made-up string.
  - **A live divergence, found by refactoring (D-051).** Extracting the shared §2/§4.0 field rules into `fields` on both sides exposed that the reference accepted a CBOR `true` wherever a uint was required — `isinstance(True, int)` is true in Python — while Go refused it. The two implementations disagreed about whether `{"expires": true}` is a valid `enroll` body, and **no vector covered it, so nothing failed.** Both refuse now, and `requests-bad/bool-expires` binds the next implementation. This is why the oracle gets refactored rather than admired.
  - **`make vectors` was destroying the Go half of the suite (D-052).** Every run deleted `served/` and `proofs/` — eleven files — because prune removes what the run did not write, and 2.7's two-provenance split had reached `vectors-check` without reaching the generator. Pruning is now scoped to declared `OWNED` paths, a path in neither half **stops the run**, and three tests pin the boundary. The orphan hazard keeps coming back from a new direction; this time the fix is a rule that fails loudly instead of a habit.
  - **A third stale worked number.** §12 said the replay fixture was **82 entries**; it has been **91** since 1.x. Same failure as 2.8's fingerprint, one table away. `internal/specdoc` now checks the count against `manifest.json` too — every number SPEC.md quotes from the suite is now either derived or guarded.
  - 26 request vectors: 4 positives (including a 64-byte `device_id` and non-ASCII labels) and **22 negatives across all four layers** — text, CBOR profile, field rules, and signature. Among them `forged-signature`, structurally perfect and signed by another key: without it a package that never calls Ed25519 passes the whole directory, which is exactly what gate run 4 found in the entry vectors.
  - Go: 22 packages, 149 tests. Python: 196 tests. `make ci`, staticcheck, both halves of `vectors-check` green; module graph still 7.
- **2026-09-19 · 2.9b-i the signer seam and the ssh-agent — a hand-written client is only allowed if a real agent tests it.**
  - **The seam is a stdlib interface, not a Norn one (D-054).** `entry.Sign` now takes a `crypto.Signer`; `ed25519.PrivateKey` already satisfies it, so **every existing call site compiled unchanged** while a key held by a TKey or 1Password became usable for the first time. Ed25519 is enforced *at* the seam: a P-256 signer — Secure Enclave and TPM 2.0 offer exactly that, so someone will try it — is refused with an error rather than a panic, and a signer that returns the wrong number of bytes leaves the envelope untouched instead of writing a malformed `sigs` entry.
  - **Why the client is ours (D-053), with numbers.** `x/crypto/ssh/agent` measured at **five modules** (crypto, net, sys, term, text) plus the whole SSH transport, for a protocol Norn uses **four messages** of. Norn's graph is 7 and its pitch is a NAS and a Pi; same trade as D-049, and the graph is still 7 after this checkpoint.
  - **And why that is not the usual self-agreement trap.** The real objection to hand-writing a wire format is that the author tests it against their own fake and learns nothing. So the tests drive **OpenSSH's `ssh-agent`**: `ssh-keygen` makes an Ed25519 key, `ssh-add` loads it, and this package lists it, signs an entry through it, and the result verifies as an ordinary §4.2 signature — the same discipline as `transparency-dev/formats` parsing our checkpoints. `NORN_REQUIRE_SSH_AGENT=1` in CI turns "not installed" into a **failure**, so the real-agent tests cannot quietly stop running on every platform at once. The fake agent keeps the cases a real one will not perform on request: signing with the wrong key, announcing a gigabyte, answering with the wrong message type, claiming another algorithm.
  - **A signature from an agent is verified before it is used.** The agent is a separate process, sometimes another vendor's, sometimes hardware. If it hands back something that does not verify, that has to fail in the CLI rather than in somebody else's replay, where it would look like a Norn bug. The fake-agent test that proves it signs with a *different* key and expects a refusal.
  - Keys of other types in the same agent are **skipped, not refused**: the user's RSA login key sitting next to a Norn signer is the normal case, and failing there would make Norn unusable on a real workstation.
  - Go: 23 packages, 169 tests. `make ci`, staticcheck and both halves of `vectors-check` green; module graph still **7**.
- **2026-09-19 · 2.9b-ii the key file — the measurement inverted the plan, so the plan changed (D-055).** `ENROLLMENT.md` promised tier 0 as an "age-style scrypt" file. Implementing it found three things wrong with that, in ascending order of importance.
  - **The dependency measurement says the obvious answer is not the cheap one.** `x/crypto/scrypt` **alone** pulls the same **five modules** as the whole of `x/crypto/ssh` — the cost is x/crypto's own `go.mod`, not the package you import. "A small KDF" was never cheaper than "the entire OpenSSH key format"; it was the same price for less. Norn's graph is still **7** because neither was adopted.
  - **It breaks a promise the project makes in writing.** `ENROLLMENT.md` part 1 says Norn has "no key format to invent" — and an age-style envelope around an Ed25519 seed is a key format, owned forever. The OpenSSH private-key format already exists, so tier 0 is now literally the file `ssh-keygen` writes.
  - **And it does not fit the threat model.** The file exists because `nornd` signs `rotate` and self-`revoke` **at boot with nobody at the keyboard**; a passphrase would have to sit beside the key. So encrypted keys are **refused**, with an error naming the remedy (`ssh-add`), and a human's signer key belongs in an agent — where a passphrase-protected key ends up anyway, after one prompt.
  - **Tier 0 becomes tier 1 with no conversion, and that is a test rather than a claim:** `ssh-add` loads a key `norn` wrote into a **real agent**, and the agent then lists exactly that key. Both directions of the format are checked against the real tools — `ssh-keygen -y` reads what Norn writes, Norn reads what `ssh-keygen` writes — under D-053's rule: **hand-write wire formats, never crypto primitives.** Unencrypted openssh-key-v1 is pure framing; the encrypted kind needs bcrypt-pbkdf, and refusing it is what keeps the rule intact.
  - **Three copies of the public key travel inside that file, and they must agree.** A file whose halves disagree is damaged or crafted, and signing with it would put an unexpected identity into the log. Also refused: a key file other users can read (the error names the mode), a second `Write` over an existing key (overwriting one destroys the identity `rotate` and self-`revoke` depend on, and the log cannot give it back), and **every truncation of the blob, at every offset** — a key file is no more trusted an input than an agent socket.
  - `internal/sshwire` now owns the RFC 4251 §5 encoding both the agent and the key file speak, for the same reason `fields` owns the §2 rules: the second copy of "check this length before using it as a bound" is the one that is wrong.
  - Go: 25 packages, 183 tests; module graph still **7**. `make ci`, staticcheck and both halves of `vectors-check` green.
- **2026-09-19 · 2.9c `norn enroll` — the device side, where a format meets a person.**
  - **WireGuard keys are pinned to RFC 7748's own vectors.** Deriving a public key wrongly is the quietest possible bug: the `enroll` entry would be perfectly valid, every signature would verify, and the tunnel would simply never come up. The arithmetic is `crypto/ecdh`'s (stdlib, no dependency), and the tests check Alice's and Bob's keys from the RFC — `wg` is not installed here, so the specification is the oracle instead of the tool.
  - **stdout is the request and nothing else**, so `norn enroll … > request.txt` yields exactly the request; the summary, the guidance and the QR go to stderr, where they cannot corrupt that file. The QR is drawn only when stderr is a terminal, so a pipe never fills with escape codes.
  - **The command checks its own work before a human acts on it:** the request it just built is decoded and verified before printing. A request that does not verify is a bug here, and it must not leave the machine.
  - **The QR carries the uppercase form (D-056).** §16.2 allows uppercase because QR alphanumeric mode has no lowercase letters, and the test **measures** the saving rather than assuming it. An end-to-end test scans-by-proxy: the uppercase text must decode to the same request, or the camera path silently does not work.
  - **What Norn owns in a QR is the part the library cannot check** — the quiet zone and the light/dark mapping. A code with no quiet zone, or inverted, is a valid QR no scanner reads. `Matrix` is therefore separate from the drawing and checked module-for-module against `rsc.io/qr`'s own map, with the quiet zone asserted on all four sides and terminal colours written explicitly (half-blocks alone invert on a light-background terminal). **Honest limit:** no QR *decoder* exists on this machine, so nothing here proves a phone reads it — that is a `PLAN.md` Phase 2 gate line and it stays open.
  - The summary states plainly what the request does **not** prove: the WireGuard key is X25519, so nothing in the request shows the device holds it (§16.1). A tool that overstates its evidence is the failure this project keeps finding in its own prose.
  - A device enrolling for the first time has no trust file, so `-net` takes an origin (`norn/…`) or 32 hex digits, and `trust.NetFromOrigin` is the new inverse of `OriginFor`, pinned by a round-trip property. `-trust` works too for a device being re-enrolled, and **the two disagreeing is a refusal, not a guess**.
  - Go: 27 packages, 208 tests; module graph 7 → **8**. `make ci`, staticcheck and both halves of `vectors-check` green.

## Phase 3 — The enforcement agent

`ENFORCEMENT.md` part 1 is the whole idea: WireGuard decides whom to talk to in
exactly one place, the cryptokey routing table, and Norn enforces **there and
nowhere else**. No packet-path code, no handshake changes, no protocol of its
own — a rogue key is simply never installed, or is removed.

Every line of this phase's `PLAN.md` gate is a **measurement**: a p99 over a
thousand runs, two 24-hour soaks, a real NetBird server, a Tailscale netmap
event. So the code can be built and proven correct here, and the gate cannot
close outside the lab — the same shape as Phase 2, and worth saying before
starting rather than after.

| # | Checkpoint | Done when | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | `internal/peertable` | the narrow seam Norn touches — peers in, peers out — with a fake that records what a real interface would have been told | ✅ |
| 3.2 | `internal/reconcile` | observe, owner and watchdog as **pure decisions** over (actual, desired): no I/O, so every case including the A1 swap attack is a unit test | ✅ |
| 3.3 | `internal/endpoint` | providers that supply endpoints and allowed-ips but are **untrusted for keys**: a key they name that is not proven is dropped and logged | ✅ |
| 3.4 | `/run/norn/proven.json` | the verifier→enforcer interface of `ENFORCEMENT.md` part 9, written atomically, with its schema pinned | ✅ |
| 3.5 | `nornd` | the daemon; split | ✅ |
| 3.5a | `internal/agent` | one verify-and-reconcile cycle, and the failure semantics of `ENFORCEMENT.md` part 8 — above all, **a failed verification never widens or empties the peer table** | ✅ |
| 3.5b | `internal/wgdev` | the real interface behind the same seam. **Moved ahead of the daemon:** a `nornd` with nothing to drive cannot be run, and the dependency question had to be answered before a binary depended on the answer | ✅ |
| 3.5c | `cmd/nornd` | the binary: config, signals, the poll loop, and **observe as the default** (D-005) | ✅ |
| 3.6 | Fight detection and quarantine | N evictions in W → `CONTROL_PLANE_FIGHT`; `quarantine` fails closed **by choice, never by default** | ✅ |
| 3.8 | Phase 3 gate audit | each line read against what is actually tested, and what the lab still owes | ✅ |

## Phase 4 — Witnesses, gossip, freshness

`GOSSIP.md` part 1 in one sentence: **witnesses guard against the log; gossip
guards against the witnesses.** Neither alone is enough, and together the only
undetectable attack is a log plus a witness quorum showing *every* node the
same false history — which is no longer a split view but a forgery of signed
entries, and that needs signer keys.

This phase also settles two debts the earlier phases wrote down rather than
hid: **§10 step 3**, the witness-policy check the verifier still does not do
(2.9e-i), and **`freshness: "unknown"`** in `proven.json` (3.4), which stays
unknown until something cosigns. It closes **2.6b** too — an unmodified
`transparency-dev/witness` cosigning a Norn checkpoint.

| # | Checkpoint | Done when | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1a | Cosignature keys | witness keys are **cosignature** keys (algorithm 0x04), not plain Ed25519 note keys — today Norn refuses the only kind a real witness publishes | ✅ |
| 4.1b | Policy parsing | `tlog-policy` parses to the real grammar, a quorum evaluates over a set of cosigners, and the trust file's `witnesses` and `policy` must agree | ✅ |
| 4.1c | The verifier enforces the quorum | cosigned vectors, and a checkpoint that does not satisfy the policy is **refused** — §10 step 3, finally | ✅ |
| 4.2a | `quorum_time` | the latest instant the policy is satisfied — the k-th newest cosignature generalised to groups, since a nested policy has no single k | ✅ |
| 4.2b | The freshness machine | `fresh → degraded → hard_stale` on **monotonic** age from witness time, in `proven.json` and `norn status` | ✅ |
| 4.2c | `CLOCK_SKEW` | the wall clock is compared to witness time and never decides anything — an alarm, not a state change (A11) | ✅ |
| 4.2d | `degraded` and `hard_stale` are **acted on** | the 5-minute alarm cadence, and the enforcer dropping every peer past S_hard — with the `nornd` flag that makes the state reachable at all | ✅ |

## Phase 5 — Attack demos + monitor

Phase 5 has two halves and they are not alike. **`norn monitor` is software**,
and every rule in `LAB.md` §3 can be written and tested here. **The demos are a
lab**: `make lab-up`, containers, a patched Headscale and NetBird, a phone
receiving a push, and tapes rendered for a README. Nothing in this repository
can produce those, so the checkpoints below build the monitor and the gate
audit says plainly what the lab still owes.

The monitor is also the one component that is *allowed* to be wrong without
anyone being harmed: it never sits on the enforcement path (`LAB.md` §3). That
is why it can poll witnesses, hold a receipt inbox and talk to `ntfy` — none of
which a node may do.

| # | Checkpoint | Done when | ✔ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1 | The rules engine | `LAB.md` §3's table as code: an observation in, a level and a sentence out, with the thresholds a homelab can change | ✅ |
| 5.2 | Watching a network | the log, the witnesses and each node's `/norn/checkpoint` and `/norn/evidence` — read-only, over the tunnel, as an enrolled peer | ✅ |
| 5.3 | The receipt inbox | a receipt whose deadline passed with no inclusion is **non-repudiable proof of A2**, and the monitor is what notices | ✅ |
| 5.4 | Outputs | stdout JSON always; `ntfy`, Home Assistant, Alertmanager and email optional and each failing alone | ✅ |
| 5.5 | The status page | read-only HTML on the tunnel address: sizes, ages, witness times, the device table and the last entries in plain words | ✅ |
| 5.6 | `norn monitor` | the command, its config, and one run that produces a notification per rule | ✅ |
| 5.7 | Phase 5 gate audit | each line against what is tested, and the demos named as the lab's | ✅ |
| 5.8 | `norn audit --by` | what a stolen signer key did: every entry a given key signed, since a given time — `ENROLLMENT.md` R2's first step | ✅ |

## Phase 6 — Spec v1 + publication

Phase 6 is three gate lines and two of them need **people**: somebody outside
this homelab running the lab and filing an issue, and somebody who has run at
least two of Tailnet Lock, Nebula and NetBird reviewing the comparison table.
Nothing here can manufacture either, and pretending otherwise would be the
exact failure the cold-model gates were invented to prevent.

The third — *"cold-model gate repeated on frozen spec: independent verifier
passes all vectors"* — is a **process**, and it is the one the project has run
three times already. It needs a reader with no memory of writing the thing,
which is the whole point.

So: freeze the spec honestly, make the vectors usable by somebody who does not
have this repository, write what a stranger needs to decide whether Norn is for
them, and then run the gate.

The why is written out: a signature binds the target, not the source; `dup-entry` catches only identical bytes and the current-key check only a changed identity key; the five withheld-entry cases from the discussion are the examples. The owner took it further than the rotate: the same withheld-entry pattern reinstates a removed signer (two signed "add X" entries, one withheld, X later removed for compromise), reverts a retired log key, revokes a re-enrolled id, re-admits a revoked one. **3-B′:** every state-changing entry is an authenticated compare-and-swap — `prev`, the index of the last accepted entry that changed the object it modifies (a device record; the signer set with its threshold; the root set with its; `params`; `policy`; `log_key`; 0 for what the genesis defines, absent only for an id never seen), refused `stale-state` when it is not the object's current version, checked after decode, lookup and the signature checks. An index was chosen over a record hash: it is monotonic, it points at the exact event, and it binds the whole record because any change to any field is itself an entry that bumps it. The no-op rule the owner first proposed was withdrawn; under CAS a stale no-op cannot land either. **6-A as one invariant:** active log keys ∩ active witness keys = ∅ on public-key bytes, enforced at trust-file load, at a `policy` entry and at a `log_key` entry (`dup-key`, widened), because a valid trust file could otherwise be turned into a self-cosigning log by a later entry. Accept and reword, or refuse: D-077.

The variant that refuses the log as `entries` is the reading the prose will rule out.

A hash tile longer than 32 × W fails `checkTiles`'s `bytes.Equal`: `tiles`, row 12's "disagrees with the rebuilt tree", with "byte for byte, length included" added so nobody reads the first 32 × W bytes and stops.
  - **M4 is a decision, a short one.** `cosign.Verify` casts the eight timestamp bytes to `int64` and `Message` renders `time %d`, so a witness's cosignature over `time 9223372036854775808` fails the signature check and is `cosignature` — the answer D-076's "one bound for every decimal line" wants, reached by a cast rather than a rule, as the receipt deadline was before 6.7-r-f-d. - **6.5l-ix-f-b-ii — `nornd` reads `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` on Linux, so a suspend counts in §15's age; Go's monotonic reading elsewhere, the gap named (Opus).**
  - **Why.** §15's age is witness time plus monotonic time since the view was learned. `nornd` handed the agent no clock, so the agent's default — Go's monotonic reading, `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux — was used, and that clock stops while the machine is suspended: a node that slept for an hour judged its view an hour younger than it was, the direction D-074 (b)'s review found the clock already erring in.
  - **The change.** `cmd/nornd/mono.go`: `clockFor(goos)` names the clock — `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` (id 7) on Linux, Go's monotonic reading elsewhere — with the gap stated in its comment; `mono_linux.go` reads it with `unix.ClockGettime`, from zero at start, repeating the last reading rather than mixing clocks if the kernel ever refused one; `mono_other.go` is Go's reading. The id is restated as `bootTimeID` so the choice is testable on any platform, and the Linux build checks it equals `unix.CLOCK_BOOTTIME` with two constant array lengths that cannot both be non-negative unless they are equal. `build` hands the reading to the agent through `newMono`. `golang.org/x/sys` is now a direct dependency (it was already in the graph through `wgctrl`, same version; `go.sum` unchanged).

This one fires only where a restart would refuse (`owner` and `watchdog` without `allow_no_quorum`, 033r-a's reading) and says what *that* is about: the node is enforcing on the log operator's word alone, it keeps enforcing, and its next start will refuse unless the setting is given. Two alarms with two meanings, each countable; so `NO_QUORUM`, at error level in `nornd` (the condition is an outage waiting for a restart), in `LAB.md`'s alarm table.

Said once on entering the condition and again every `DegradedAlarmEvery`, as `degraded` is; raising the quorum again ends it and the next lowering is announced at once. Nothing else in the cycle looks at it: reconciliation, the proven set and the mirror go on as before.

- **6.5m-sec-023r-f — the review of §3.1 (Mythos): the text holds against both predicates, the CCTV table and Norn's vectors; every flag now traces to its clause as a test; one finding, put to the owner as a DECISION rather than patched — item 2's "wherever a key is admitted" and its enumeration disagree about two keys; two nits, no patch.**
  - **Item 1, clause by clause.** Go: `decodeCanonical` (decodes and re-encodes to the same bytes: refuses `y ≥ p` and `x = −0`) and `primeOrder` (`P ≠ O` and `[L−1]P + P = O`, since `L` is the zero scalar). The reference: libsodium's `crypto_core_ed25519_is_valid_point` — canonical by `y < p`, a blocklist of the small-order encodings compared with the sign bit masked, on the curve, in the main subgroup. The two are not the same algorithm and agree on every point: a non-canonical encoding can name only `y < 19` or `x = −0`, no such point has order `L` (c-i's exhaustive test), and the only points with `x = 0` are the identity and the order-2 point, so the blocklist refuses the `x = −0` encodings that re-encoding refuses. The CCTV set carries those encodings (168 vectors), and both suites agree on all 914.
  - **Item 3.** Go: `S` by `SetCanonicalBytes` (below `L`, never reduced), `k` by `SetUniformBytes(SHA-512(R ‖ A ‖ M))` over the bytes as given — canonical, since `point(A)` passed — and `[S]B − [k]A = R` by `VarTimeDoubleScalarBaseMult`. The reference: `S < L` as an integer, then libsodium's verify, which is cofactorless; with `A` and `R` of order `L` either equation is the definition's. Item 4's counts, checked: 913 refused, 305 accepted, deciding flags `non_canonical_R` 264, `non_canonical_A` 226, `low_order_A` 212, `low_order_R` 106, `low_order_component_A` 98, `low_order_component_R` 7; no CCTV vector has `S ≥ L`, as it says. Item 2's seven named points are checked in both implementations (c-iii-a, c-iii-b, d) and each has 023r-e's vector. Item 5 is true of both signers.
  - **The tracing, as a test.** `TestEveryCCTVFlagTracesToTheClauseThatRefusesIt` (`internal/ed25519v1`): for each vector and each of `A` and `R`, `non_canonical_X` ⇔ `decodeCanonical` refuses; `low_order_X` ⇔ `[8]P = O`; `low_order_component_X` ⇔ not of order `L` and not the identity (the README flags the identity `low_order` alone); no flag ⇔ `ValidPoint`; `low_order_residue` only with a component flag, `reencoded_k` only with a non-canonical one, and `cases.json` never lets either decide. It passed on its first run — it traces what c-i built — and the controls show it can fail (`ed25519v1.go` restored, `cmp`): the canonical comparison dropped, 542 mismatches from vector 8; `primeOrder` always true, 2588. One thing it makes explicit: `cases.json`'s `flag` is the first flag in §3.1's listing, not the order a verifier evaluates — Go looks at `A` before `R`, so a vector deciding on `non_canonical_R` with a low-order `A` falls at `A`; the named clause refuses it either way.

- **6.5l-ix-f-b — one checkpoint age, §15's, reviewed: the review found the clock behind it moving backwards, fixed it, vectored the three readings, and stated the boundaries and the bound's gap (Mythos; D-074 (b)). Found in review: row 6.5l-ix-f-b-ii.**
  - **The question.** §8.1's condition 4 defined `elapsed` as the monotonic time since the node learned *this* checkpoint's quorum time; §15 defined a checkpoint's age as the node's estimate of now minus its quorum time. They agree only while the held head carries the newest quorum time seen; a grown head cosigned by slower witnesses is `fresh` under the first and `degraded` under the second, and §13.2 empties the table under one reading and not the other. D-074 (b) took §15's after a Mythos review of its time source and boundaries.
  - **What the review found.** `Clock.Observe` kept the newest *quorum time*, which is not the largest *bound*: every verified pair (quorum time `q`, learned at monotonic `m`) is a lower bound on witness time now, `q + (now − m)`, and a head cosigned at a newer instant but learned long after an older one carries a smaller bound. Taking it moved the estimate backwards — exactly the direction §15 forbids for an older time — and the held view then looked younger than the node had already proven the world to be. With `S` = 900: a head at 9900 learned at 0, then one at 10000 learned at 500, read at 1000: the old clock said age 600 and `fresh`; the largest bound says 1000 and `degraded`. `Observe` now keeps the observation with the larger `q − m`; nothing else in the package changes, and the simulator's T5 and T6 pass unchanged.
  - **The text.** §8.1 condition 4 points at §15's age and says what it is not; the comparisons are `>` as durations at `S` and `S_hard`, so an age exactly on either is fresh, as the table already vectored; `CLOCK_SKEW` changes no state. §15 defines the estimate as the largest of the lower bounds, says an age is never negative (the held head's own pair is a bound), and states the bound's gap instead of hiding it: a suspend, and the time between the clock file's last write and the next start, are not counted, so the states err toward `fresh` by at most that gap until the next verified checkpoint — and a node SHOULD read a monotonic source that counts suspended time where the platform has one, which is row **6.5l-ix-f-b-ii** for `nornd` (`CLOCK_BOOTTIME` on Linux). Wall time stays out in both directions: a forward jump aging a view would let a wrong clock drop every peer, which is what A11 forbids.
  - **The vectors.** `detect/staleness.json` gains three `observed` cases — (quorum time, learned-at) pairs, `now`, the held head, the derived `elapsed` and the state — one for each reading it separates: §8.1's old definition (reads 100, says `fresh`), "newest quorum time wins" (reads 600, says `fresh`), and an older time not moving the estimate back. `elapsed` is carried as well as derived, so the cold verifier's harness, which reads `elapsed` alone, still passes every case. Written by the generator; `make vectors-log` and `vectors-sums`.

Controls, `clock.go` held in memory and restored (`cmp`): the newest quorum time winning again fails that case; every observation replacing the estimate fails `later-head-older-quorum-time` and `older-quorum-time-does-not-move-the-estimate-back` on their ages, and the package's own `TestAnOlderObservationDoesNotMoveTheClockBack` with them. One existing guard pinned the phrase "monotonic elapsed" in §15; the bound is now worded with it, and the gate ran again. README 1124 tests.

- **6.5m-sec-023r-a — NORN-ED25519-v1 as normative text: one predicate under which every library gives the same answer, in SPEC §3.1 and guarded (Mythos; the first of 023r's six sittings).**
  - **The split into sittings.** **a** this text; **b** the C2SP CCTV vectors vendored with provenance and an outcome table; **c** Go, `internal/ed25519v1`, every verification and admission site through it; **d** the reference through libsodium's point check (Codex); **e** Norn's own edge vectors from the generators (Codex); **f** a Mythos review before the parent ticks. The sub-rows say what each is done when.
  - **The predicate** (§3.1). A *valid point* is the canonical RFC 8032 §5.1.3 encoding of a point of order exactly `L`: `y < p`, the sign bit 0 when `x` is 0, on the curve, not the identity, no component of order 2, 4 or 8 — `[L]P = O` and `P ≠ O`. Every public key is a valid point wherever a key is admitted (genesis, `root_add`, `signer_add`, `log_key`, `enroll`, an enrollment request, a trust file's keys) or it is `decode`. A signature verifies only if `R` is a valid point, `S < L` as an integer, and `[S]B = R + [k]A`; with `A` and `R` of order `L` the cofactored equation gives the same answer, because the difference lies in the prime-order subgroup, so a verifier may compute either and the cofactorless one is the definition. PureEdDSA, no context. A verifier MUST NOT accept what the predicate refuses nor refuse what it accepts, whatever its library does. Signing is unchanged.
  - **Why order exactly `L`, not "not small order".** libsodium and ed25519-dalek's `verify_strict` stop at small-order points; a point with a small-order *component* and a prime-order one is exactly where the two equations part, and a signer holding such a key can make a signature one library accepts and another refuses. An honest key `[s]B` and an honest `R = [r]B` never have such a component, so excluding it costs nothing honest and removes every formula-dependent case. The CCTV README names this class the one `verify_strict` still accepts; §3.1 says it is excluded and why.
  - **The CCTV set, read** (fetched under D-072 (c)'s leave: `C2SP/CCTV` `ed25519/`, commit `50a8ecf2`, 2026-09-25, BSD-3-Clause, 914 vectors, SHA-256 `b38e84ca…`). Every flag is traced to the clause that rejects it: `low_order_*` and `non_canonical_*` are not valid points; `low_order_component_*` are not of order exactly `L`; `low_order_residue` and `reencoded_k` each also carry one of those. **913 vectors are rejected and one — number 305, no flag — is accepted**; the text says so by number rather than "every vector", because a predicate that rejects honest signatures is as wrong as one that accepts forgeries. No CCTV vector has `S ≥ L`; Norn's own vectors (023r-e) cover that edge. The files are in the scratchpad for 023r-b to vendor; nothing third-party is in the tree yet.
  - **What the libraries do today**, so c and d are built against facts rather than hope: Go's `crypto/ed25519` is cofactorless, refuses `S ≥ L` and a non-canonical `R`, and accepts small-order and mixed-order keys (the README's "ref10" behaviour), so the Go predicate is implemented explicitly with `filippo.io/edwards25519` — canonical as "decodes and re-encodes to the same bytes", order `L` as `[2²⁵²]P + [L − 2²⁵²]P = O`; PyNaCl 1.6.2 exposes `crypto_core_ed25519_is_valid_point`, which is the predicate's point rule exactly (canonical, on the curve, main subgroup, not small order), and the reference adds `S < L` itself. The cold verifier is cofactored and checks none of this: 023r-e's vectors will fail under it, the second finding of 021r-b's kind, answered by the same new cold run.
  - **Guarded, red first.** `TestKeysDefineOneEd25519Predicate` (specdoc) requires §3 to send every signature to §3.1 and §3.1 to state the twelve sentences the code and the vectors will be built to; red before the text. §12.1's not-vectored list names the predicate as stated and not yet vectored, with the rows that vector it. Two `RFC 8032 §…` citations had wrapped across a line, which the cross-reference checker reads as internal sections; joined. README 1122 tests.
  - **Gate:** generators first, no change under `testdata/`; `make test` (race) alone, 51 packages `ok`; `vectors-check`, 237 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet`, `verify-py` (1474 checks, 0 FAIL) clean.
- **6.5m-sec-021r-a — D-072 (a) as normative text: on a proven fork a node keeps enforcing the devices proven both at the common prefix and at its own held head, shrinks and never grows, fails closed without a common prefix, and the evidence (version 2) carries the split so a bystander can do the same (Mythos; the first of 021r's four sittings).**
  - **The split into sittings.** 021r is a protocol change, an evidence-format change, an agent change and a simulator change; one sitting each, in that order, so every later one builds on text already guarded: **a** this text; **b** `forkevidence` version 2 and the vectors (Codex); **c** the agent's frozen set, through one path for the detector, the bystander and the restart; **d** the simulator's T1/T1b and the documents (Codex). The sub-rows say what each is done when.
  - **The rule, as written** (§11 rules 2–4, §13.2). A node that proved a fork adopts no checkpoint under its anchor; every cycle it enforces the **frozen set** — the devices proven at the common prefix *and* at the head the node holds, with the routes their enrollment granted as of the prefix — so the set may stay the same or shrink and never grows: what either branch added after the split goes, what this branch revoked after it stays out; `owner` and `watchdog` evict against it, `observe` reports. With no common prefix — the evidence claims none, or the node's own branch does not reach the split or has another root there — the desired set is empty, as past `S_hard`: a fork is proof the log and a quorum misbehaved, and unlike staleness it gets no benefit of the doubt. `FORK` is critical and repeats on the degraded cadence, saying what is kept and what was removed. The paragraph that follows the rules says what rule 3 used to say and why it was wrong (audit SEC-021): a frozen watchdog stopped evicting, and the rogue a split view is for stayed connected after the node had proved the split.
  - **Why "proven at the prefix and at the held head" rather than "what was on the interface".** The second is what the node enforced per its own branch, and it is recomputable from the mirror after a reboot; an interface snapshot is not, and a watchdog's interface holds things it never authorized. Routes from the split state's grant, the bound both branches agreed to.
  - **The evidence** (§11.1, version 2): `split` (the common entry prefix, as the accuser computed it from the two trees it held), `split_root`, and a consistency proof from (`split`, `split_root`) to each signed head — eleven keys, a fifth reader step, `proof` and `schema` codes extended, no new code. A version-1 file still proves a fork exactly as before and claims no split, so a reader fails closed on it; a node writes version 2. **An accuser can understate the split and never overstate it**: the two proofs hold at every size up to the true split and at none above, so no maximality proof is carried — understating is dominated by the fork itself, since whoever can sign a fork can fork at entry 1, which D-072 (a) already accepts as the attacker's new button.
  - **The cold verifier.** `contrib/verify-py` is sealed at `89b5b99` and refuses version 2 as `version`. Nothing fails today — no version-2 file exists yet — but when 021r-b's vectors land, `make verify-py` fails on them. That is the finding H14's rule anticipates for the first normative change after the freeze, answered by a new cold run and never by editing the verifier; recorded in D-072's design notes and in 021r-b's row.
  - **Guarded, red first.** `TestAProvenForkShrinksToTheCommonPrefix` (specdoc) requires the fifteen sentences the agent, the reader and the simulator will be built to — six in §11, eight in §11.1, §13.2's — and failed on all fifteen before the text. The fork vectors' generator quotes §11.1's `version` row as the rule behind `bad-wrong-version`; the quote moved with the row, `make vectors-log` rewrote that one line of `fork/cases.json` and nothing else, and `make vectors-sums` the checksum. SPEC's preamble now names the one normative change since the freeze, dated. README 1121 tests.

There is no witness server in this tree, so three modelled honest witnesses that hold A answer through the real `witness.Client` and `Submitter`: each first corrects the log's stated old size (`409`, the retry `ConflictError` drives), then refuses B (`422`), and the submitter reports all three as "could not verify consistency". - **6.5m-xii-m — the mirror keeps the current head and one previous generation of partial tiles, and deletes the rest after the new checkpoint is durable; the client reads a bundle at its exact width first (Codex lane AB, `gpt-6.1-sol`, high; integrated). Found while integrating: row 6.5m-xii-s.**
  - **Why.** H13 found that `mirror.Write` never removed a file: every head a node adopted left its partial entry bundle and partial hash tiles behind — about 58 GB per node at 10⁶ entries against 0.45 GB for the current head (`THREAT-MODEL.md` §6.1's second table).
  - **What is deleted, and when.** After the new checkpoint has been written durably — never before, so a crash leaves extra files rather than a checkpoint naming missing ones — `prunePartials` removes every partial bundle and partial hash tile that belongs to neither the new head nor the head the mirror held just before it. The previous head's size comes from the checkpoint file the mirror already reads; if that file does not parse, nothing is pruned that time. The previous generation stays because a peer that read the old checkpoint a moment ago is fetching its exact paths, and `checkTiles` has no fallback. A path is eligible only if it round-trips through `tlog`'s own path functions as a canonical partial (`tile/<L>/…/<N>.p/<W>`, `tile/entries/…/<N>.p/<W>`, widths 1–255) — never a full tile, the checkpoint, or a lookalike; the walk runs inside an `os.Root`, so neither a symlink nor a directory swapped mid-walk reaches outside the mirror. A removal error is returned; a file already gone is not one.
  - **The client change, and why it is not a rule change.** `fetchBundle` tried the full bundle first. With the previous generation kept, a peer verifying head 255 after the mirror moved to 256 got the new full bundle — 256 entries for a checkpoint of 255 — and refused a head it should accept. It now asks for the checkpoint's exact width first and the full bundle second; what it accepts and refuses is unchanged (the count check stays), only which file it reads first.

  - **The one difference the nones follow from:** KEYTRANS keeps the authority to change a label outside the log and records what it did; Norn puts the authority inside the log so that it is transparent too — which is why the state is global and every node replays everything. A Norn entry as a KEYTRANS value would need its client to replay every other label's governance to know whether its signatures counted: full replication through a dictionary built to avoid it.
  - **Where each *none* belongs**, as the plan asks: the grant in a WireGuard integration layer; revocation, governance and freshness-as-requirements in a separate authorization document; enforcement as implementation policy; fork evidence as a Norn extension of the architecture's "non-repudiable proof".

A consequence worth stating: under `granted`, gossip reaches only devices with a grant, because a node addresses peers through their allowed-ips — 6.11-c says so.

The enrollment's `ip` label was D-026's "advisory hint"; it is now the **grant**: split on commas, each part parsed as a prefix and masked, duplicates removed, sorted as text; a label that does not parse *as a whole* is no grant (a bound with a hole in it is not the bound the signers signed), and an IPv4-mapped IPv6 prefix is no grant because the two implementations would render it differently and a grant is compared as text. `params.routes` ∈ {`granted`, `advisory`}, default `granted`, is the one text-valued parameter and its value set is closed. - **6.5l-ix-b — run 13's eight protocol questions, one DECISION block with a recommendation each (open, D-074 when answered).**
  - **What it is.** The questions 6.5l-ix-a's triage classed as *protocol* — D2 (what key verifies a bundle or receipt after a log-key rotation), D5 (two definitions of a checkpoint's age), D6 (whose signed-note rules win, lines from keys nobody holds, UTF-8), D7 ("the same keys": text or public key), D8 (a directive after `quorum`), D10 (the key id's case and "a Unicode space"), D12 (no code for a served log whose entry 0 is not the genesis), D13 (CBOR simple values) — each with what both implementations do today, verified in the tree rather than recalled: `proof.Bundle.Check` and `norn submit` under the trust file's key alone; `agent.freshness` is §15's; `note.Verify` and `cosign.Verify` match name and key id before applying a length; both trust validators compare whole verifier-key text; both policy parsers accept a directive after `quorum`; both accept lowercase key ids only; the two whitespace predicates diverge on U+001C–U+001F; `checkGenesis` refuses with a plain error; both decoders refuse the other simple values.
  - **The recommendations**, all the first option: verify bundles and receipts under the verifier's trusted keys and current policy; §15's age, stated once; write what the verifiers do and require UTF-8; the same verifier key as text; any line order; lowercase hex and the Unicode `White_Space` property; a `genesis` code made by the verifier; simple values forbidden. Four change code (a, c, f, g) and each will be one sitting of H5-f; the rest are prose and vectors. Nothing changes a wire format.

- **6.5l-ix-d-i — the receipt order is held pair by pair, and an unpadded leaf hash is refused. H5-d split into i–iii.**
  - **Why split.** d named three kinds of work in two generators: receipts (the reference writes `receipt-bad/`), the served path and `checkpoints-bad/` (Go's `norn-genlog`), and two odd ones out — tile paths past index 999 and the trust file's origin case. One sitting each.
  - **What was missing.** §7: "a reader MUST check in this order. The first failed step decides the refusal code", and §12.1 said the order was vectored. Every `receipt-bad/` case failed one step, so a reader that swapped any two adjacent steps refused each case for the same reason and passed — run 13's six receipt survivors. And D18's `leaf-b64-unpadded-ok`: no receipt carried a leaf hash without its `=`.
  - **Seven receipts**, each re-signed by the anchored log key unless the signer is its fault:
    - `order-log-signature-before-receipt` — signed by `logkey2` and a wrong header: `log-signature`.
    - `order-receipt-before-origin` — wrong header and a foreign origin: `receipt`.
    - `order-origin-before-leaf-hash` — foreign origin and `!!!!` for the leaf hash: `origin`.
    - `order-leaf-hash-before-deadline` — `!!!!` and a leading zero on the deadline: `leaf-hash`.
    - `order-deadline-before-entry` — the leading zero and another entry's hash: `deadline`.
    - `order-entry-before-expired` — another entry's hash, checked at the deadline: `entry`.
    - `leaf-hash-unpadded` — the good hash with its `=` dropped, which a lenient decoder reads as the same 32 bytes: `leaf-hash`.
  - **A guard that cited the right rule.** The first form cited "a reader MUST check in this order" for every pair; `TestEveryServedAndBundleNegativeCitesTheRuleOfItsCode` refused that, since each case's `says` must be the rule of the step that decides it. Each now cites that step's rule, and `cases.json`'s comment says what an `order-` case is.

Red against the suite before this row: six cases absent. The existing data-driven test checks every code.
  - **Documents.** §12's `receipt-bad/` row (sixteen, the `order-` cases), §12.1's receipt-order row (what holds the order now, run 13's D4) and its leaf-hash row, and the vectors README.
  - **Seven controls**, each restored byte for byte (digests checked): in Go's `receipt.Check`, each later step moved in front of its predecessor — 3 before 2, 4 before 3, 5 before 4, 6 before 5, 7 before 6, 8 before 7 — and an unpadded leaf hash read leniently (raw decoding, compared unpadded) each fail `TestReceiptBadVectorsMatchTheirDeclaredCodes`. **Which were gaps**: applied to a copy of the tree before this row (every package but `agent`), step 3 before 2, 5 before 4, 6 before 5 and the lenient leaf hash pass everything — gaps for this implementation too. 4 before 3, 7 before 6 and 8 before 7 were held by `receipt`'s own unit tests and `norn submit`'s, which a second implementation never sees; the vectors carry them to one.

- **6.5m-sec-012 — owner mode converges on a real interface: the interface's own key is not a peer, and allowed-ips are desired masked (Codex lane L, integrated). SEC-012 and SEC-019 close.**
  - **What was wrong.** Against `peertable.Fake`, owner mode looked converged; against a kernel it would have rewritten the table every `T_poll`, for two reasons. The desired set held every proven device, the node's own among them, and the kernel and wireguard-go refuse a peer with the interface's own key — so `actual ≠ desired` forever (SEC-012); `PeerAddresses` offered the node's own address to gossip too. And no prefix was ever masked, so a hint of `10.9.0.5/24` never equalled the `10.9.0.0/24` the kernel returns (SEC-019).
  - **The lane.** `gpt-6-astra`, high — a subtle row whose real half (a kernel) cannot run here. `peertable.Device` gains `OwnKey()`, required rather than an optional assertion that could silently skip the check; `wgdev` reads the device's `PublicKey` through a three-method client seam its tests can fake. The agent leaves the own key out of the desired set and of `PeerAddresses`, keeps the device proven everywhere else (`proven.json` unchanged), and does not let its provider hints become an unproven claim or an overlap alarm. Allowed-ips are masked once, in `endpoint.Desired`, where every provider's hints become peers, without mutating the hints. `peertable.Fake` learns the kernel's two rules behind opt-in fields (`OwnPublicKey`, `MaskPrefixes`), defaults unchanged. An unreadable own key is `INTERFACE_UNAVAILABLE` and leaves the table alone; a zero key is a new event, `INTERFACE_UNCONFIGURED`, and the node reconciles against the whole proven set.
  - **Red first** (the lane's): the new kernel-like convergence gate, beside the unchanged original — "50 further writes on an unchanged kernel-like interface" — which first proves the fake really drops the own key and masks, so weakening the fake cannot quietly weaken the gate; and four behaviour tests, each red before its fix.
  - **What review changed:**
    - **The notice said itself every poll.** `INTERFACE_UNCONFIGURED` was emitted from `desired`, which reconcile and `PeerAddresses` both call: on a keyless interface, two notices per cycle for as long as it lasted, burying everything else. - **6.5m-sec-034 — `norn-log`'s HTTP server has timeouts and a header cap.**
  - **What was wrong.** The log — the one server every node and the monitor read from — served with `http.ListenAndServe`: no header, read, write or idle timeout, and Go's 1 MB header cap. A client that sent half a request line and then nothing held a connection, a goroutine and a file descriptor for as long as it liked; enough of them and the log stops answering anyone. Built here rather than in a lane, because its red test needs a listener the lane sandbox forbids.
  - **Red first, three ways**, with `newServer` as a stub that set nothing: a half-sent request (`GET /checkpoint`, a `Host` line, never the blank line) was held open for the test's full five seconds; a 64 KiB header was answered 200; and no limit was set at all.
  - **The fix.** `newServer` builds the log's server with every limit: 10 s to read the header, 30 s to read a request, a minute to write a response, two minutes idle, and a 16 KiB header cap — generous against honest use, where a header is a few hundred bytes, a submission is one entry read under `cbor.MaxEntryBytes`, and the largest response is one tile or bundle. The values are package variables so a test can shorten them, as `gossip.SetTimeout` does. Rate limiting — §7's 429 and the replay-per-submission cost — remains H11.
  - **Three controls**, each restored byte for byte (digest checked): no header timeout fails the slow-client test (and the every-limit test); no header cap fails the oversized-header test; no idle timeout fails the every-limit test, which exists because the two behavioural tests cannot see a missing write or idle timeout.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1037 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

(Audit 033's other half, refusing to enforce under `quorum none`, is row 033r and waits on D-072 e; its "security events at INFO" half was lane B's level table.)
  - **Red first.** An owner node under a `quorum none` trust file, over a log from before the fixture's `policy` entry so that every cycle verifies under `none`: no alarm at 0 s, 1 min, 4 min, 5 min, 6 min or 10 min. The first version of the test served the full fixture, whose roots publish three of three at entry 28 — after the first cycle the node verified under that and was simply fresh; the test now says why it serves twenty entries.
  - **The fix.** `reportFreshness` gains the `unknown` case: `FRESHNESS_UNKNOWN`, once on entering the state and again every `DegradedAlarmEvery` (5 min) while it lasts, the peer table kept, the message naming `quorum none` as the one policy that asks for this. `nornd` reports it at WARN (its level-table test requires every kind be placed). GOSSIP §5's state machine gains the `unknown` row. The quorum-none trust file is now a shared test helper, used by 028's test too.
  - **Two controls**, each restored byte for byte (digest checked): `unknown` saying nothing, and `unknown` said once and never repeated, each fail the cadence test.

- **6.5m-sec-028 — a head with no quorum time reads `unknown`, never `hard_stale`.**
  - **What was wrong.** §15: "A `quorum none` policy has no quorum time: freshness is `unknown`, not an assertion of recency." `agent.freshness` aged such a head from `time.Time{}`, which answers `unknown` only while the witness clock has never been set. Once anything had set it — D-071's clock file outliving a policy change and a restart, or an earlier cosigned head — the head was two thousand years old: `degraded`, and past `S_hard`, `hard_stale`, so an owner node emptied its table for a head that simply had no time.
  - **Red first, at two levels.** `freshness` on a head without quorum time, after a verified cycle had set the clock, read `degraded` (no `S_hard`) and `hard_stale` (one hour) at an age of 2,562,047 hours. And an owner node under a `quorum none` trust file — the fixture's witnesses listed and named, nobody required, since §9.1 wants at least one witness and every listed one named — with a clock file from before and `S_hard` one hour: `HARD_STALE`, every peer dropped.
  - **The fix.** A head with no quorum time is `unknown`, with no age, whatever the clock holds. The only other place that could age from the zero time was this one; the monitor and `isStale` already treat a missing quorum time as no age.
  - **One control**, restored byte for byte (digest checked): aging from the zero time again fails both tests.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1033 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-027 — a witness line of the other supported length is refused, not skipped; vector `checkpoints-bad/28` pins it.**
  - **The rule was already written.** §7: "once a line's name and key id match a trusted key, verification also checks the length for that key's algorithm … never a prefix or the other algorithm's supported length"; §10.1's `cosignature` is "a cosignature line whose name and key id match a listed witness does not verify". The log side had its check and its vector (`24`, D14c). The witness side had neither: `cosign.Verify` skipped any line that was not 76 bytes *before* matching it to a witness, so a 68-byte line under `pi`'s name and cosignature key id, beside three good lines, was ignored and the head accepted. A fix, no DECISION.
  - **Red first.** `TestAMatchedWitnessLineOfTheOtherLengthIsRefused`: two good cosignatures plus the 68-byte line returned both cosignatures and no error. **The fix**: match name and key id first, then refuse a matched line that is not a cosignature's length, as `cosignature`, with the witness's name and the line's size.
  - **The vector.** `cmd/norn-genlog` writes `checkpoints-bad/28-witness-key-other-algorithm-length` (all three good lines plus the 68-byte one), coded `cosignature`, cited in §10 ("A 68-byte payload under a listed witness's …"), §7, §10.1's row and a new §12.1 row; the vectors README says twenty-eight and names `24` and `28` together; `SHA256SUMS` regenerated by the sums target.
  - **Two guards moved, both rightly.** `TestTheSignatureBlindSetIsComputedNotAsserted` computed that a signature-blind reader *accepts* `28` — because its model applied §7's matched-key length rule to the log's key only, though its own comment says a blind reader enforces "the matched key's public algorithm length", which needs no signature. The model now applies it to every listed witness's key too, and `28` stays off `signature_blind_accepts`, beside `24`. And the README count guard's number-to-words table stopped at twenty-seven; it now reaches thirty.
  - **Three controls**, each restored byte for byte (digests checked): short witness lines skipped again (the old code) fails the unit test and, separately, the shipped vector's code check; the blind model without the witness length rule fails the blind-set guard. One mutation proves nothing and is said so: disabling only the new length check still refuses the line, as Ed25519 rejects the truncated signature — the fix's substance is not skipping a matched line, and the explicit check gives the operator the reason.
  - **Gate:** generators and the sums target first (stable on rerun), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1031 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-005bc-ii — `norn verify-evidence -log` checks a file under what the network published; SEC-005 closes. Global rule 1 now forbids every commit trailer.**
  - **The stranger's command.** A reader holding only the trust file cannot know a key the roots published after it was issued, and correctly refuses evidence signed by it; nor can it know that the roots raised the quorum. `-log URL|DIR` lets that reader learn both the way a restarted node does (D-069): the log must verify under the trust file, or — when the trust file's key or policy is what refuses it — under what its own entries publish, replayed from the pinned genesis, which is root-signed authority (§9.4); a log that verifies under neither teaches nothing. The file is then checked under the trust file's key plus every published key and the published policy, and the verdict says which (`checked by  the trust file and what … published (N log key(s))`). Without `-log` nothing changes: the trust file alone, as before.
  - **Red first, both directions.** Evidence signed by `logkey2` and cosigned by all three witnesses: refused without the log (correct), and still refused with `-log` over `served-rotated/`'s head while the flag was a stub. Evidence cosigned by two witnesses: proven under the trust file's two of three (correct), and still proven with `-log` over `served/`, whose roots raised the quorum to three — the stricter rule ignored.
  - **Three controls**, each restored byte for byte (digests checked): the published keys not used fails the rotation test; the published policy not used fails the raised-quorum test; no retry under what the log publishes fails the rotation test.
  - **SEC-005 closes** with 005a (longer-branch evidence, a freeze that cannot be lost), 005bc-i and this.
  - **Rule 1, everywhere.** The owner extended "no trailers" to every project: `~/claude-rules/CLAUDE.md` rule 1 now forbids `Co-Authored-By` and `Claude-Session` in every repo (committed there as `82a5449`, local only), the four live sessions were told, and the Norn-only memory note was retired as redundant.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1030 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-005bc-i — fork evidence is checked under the keys and policy a node verifies its log under (SEC-005 b, c); row 005bc split.**
  - **What was wrong.** `forkevidence.Check` took one log key, and all three of the agent's call sites passed the trust file's key and policy. §11.1 step 1 says a reader verifies both checkpoints "per §10", and §10 accepts the trust file's key *or* a key a state the node accepted published (§9.4), under the policy that state published — so this is the spec's own rule, unimplemented, and no DECISION. Two consequences, each red first. **(b)** a node that followed an in-log rotation to `logkey2` and then caught its log forking built evidence its own self-check refused — "evidence [], markers [1760003600.frozen]" — and after a restart called its proof something that "would not convince anybody else". **(c)** the fixture's roots raise the quorum to three of three; evidence from a peer cosigned by two witnesses was checked under the trust file's two of three, and froze the node — "two witnesses froze a node whose roots require three".
  - **The fix.** `Check(ev, origin, logVKeys []string, readerPolicy)` — every key must parse, at least one must be given, and each checkpoint must be signed by one of them (`tlog.Verify` over the set, as §10 does). The agent's `checkEvidence` passes `anchorUnder(held.State)`: the trust file's key plus every published key, and the published policy when there is one, for the self-check before filing (against the head the fork was proven against), for peer evidence, and for the freeze reloaded at start — which now runs after `restoreHead`, so a restarted node checks its evidence under what its restored head published. The informational `policy` written into evidence is the one the node was verifying under. `verify-evidence` passes the trust file's key for now; learning a network's published keys is 005bc-ii.
  - **Three controls**, each restored byte for byte (digests checked): checking under the trust file again fails both tests; loading the freeze before the head fails the reload half of the rotation test; `Check` honouring only the first key fails the rotation test.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1028 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec — the audit triage row closes; Norn commits carry no attribution trailer from here on.**
  - **The triage, fully true.** Every one of SEC-001…SEC-036 from `claude/tender-mccarthy-bzllsp` has its line in the AUDIT TRIAGE table — confirmed on master with the test or probe that shows it, fixed on master and by what, or partly fixed with what remains — and each confirmed finding has a row of its own on the hardening track. Most of those rows are now closed; the open ones (005bc, 027, 028, 033, 034, the D-072 rows and the Codex rows 012, 016 and docs) are rows, not triage. The parent's done-when is the triage, so it is ticked.

From this commit on, Norn commits end with their message: no `Co-Authored-By`, no `Claude-Session`, whatever the harness's attribution reminder says; a Codex lane's `Codex-Model` line stays, since it is the lane's report rather than attribution. `HARDENING-PLAN.md` §1 rule 6, the loop's prompt and the project memory say so. Commits already pushed keep theirs — removing them would be a force push, which the loop forbids; that waits for an explicit request.

- **6.5m-sec-035-ii — overlapping allowed-ips among proven devices are withheld and reported; SEC-035 closes.**
  - **What was wrong.** `endpoint.Desired` installed whatever allowed-ips a provider gave each proven device. Two devices with `10.9.0.0/24` and `10.9.0.2/32` were both installed, and WireGuard, routing to the most specific prefix, quietly handed one device's address to the other — a routing decision nobody signed. Lane J proved it and stopped, because reporting it needs one agent line its brief forbade; its saved test is this row's red.
  - **Red first**, three ways: the lane's test (both prefixes installed, nothing reported), a three-device case where only the overlapping prefix should go (device `a` kept both of its routes, `b` kept the overlap), and an agent-level test in which `nas` and `pi-cam` overlap and no `PROVIDER_CLAIM` named them.
  - **The fix.** `Desired` builds every peer from its hints, then `withholdOverlaps` removes from each peer every prefix that overlaps a prefix of another proven device — both sides, since choosing one would be Norn deciding — and keeps each device's other routes; a device left with no routes is `Unrouted`, as before, and is still installed, because the log proves it. `Report.Overlapping` names each pair ("host 10.9.0.2/32 overlaps subnet 10.9.0.0/24", ordered), `Empty` counts it, and the agent emits each as `PROVIDER_CLAIM`, saying why. A device's own overlapping prefixes are not a conflict between peers and are left alone. ENFORCEMENT carries the rule.
  - **Three controls**, each restored byte for byte (digests checked): overlaps reported but not withheld fails the lane's test; every route of an overlapping device withheld fails the only-the-overlap test; the agent saying nothing fails the agent test.
  - **035 closes** with 035-i (preshared keys, witness-time expiry) and this.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1026 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-iii — H3 closes: an unchanged head is a reconcile-only cycle, inherited from H4 and guarded.**
  - **What H4 left for H3.** H4-c made the agent verify from the head it holds, so an unchanged log costs one request, a grown one costs what grew, and a full verification runs every `FullVerifyEvery` (5 min) — which is H3's plan step c and the row's second clause. This row adds the two guard tests the plan names and does not rebuild: fifty cycles over an unchanged log make fifty `checkpoint` requests and no bundle or tile; a changed checkpoint is adopted on the next cycle — the appended revocation takes effect — and fetches exactly the checkpoint, the grown bundle and the grown tile.
  - **No red, and why.** Both tests passed on their first run, because the behaviour already existed; the row is a check-and-tick, as H4-c's journal said it should be. What shows the tests load-bearing is the **control**: full verification forced on every cycle fails the fifty-cycle test and leaves the adoption test green — restored byte for byte (digest checked).
  - **What was deliberately not built.** Plan step d's short-circuit — skip verification entirely when the checkpoint bytes equal the held ones — would save one fetch's signature and quorum checks per cycle, microseconds against a 200 ms poll, at the cost of a second code path through `Once`; verifying the identical note is the simpler proof that nothing changed. And the plan's "full re-verify on every gossip round": a full verification every `T_g` (30 s) at 10⁴ entries would undo most of what H4 bought; the 5-minute cadence catches a corrupt old tile (H4-c's test), and the monitor verifies in full every round regardless.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1023 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-030 — the monitor never describes a refused entry as done (Codex lane K, integrated).**
  - **What was wrong.** `readLog` described every entry that decoded in plain words — "signer … enrolled nas" — and only afterwards, in a second loop, reported the ones replay refused. An operator reading in order saw a fact and then its retraction; under D-070 a re-signed copy of a past entry is such a refused entry, so the monitor announced the SEC-001 attack as a success before saying it had failed. Red first: the fixture's refused enrolment of `nas` announced as done; a refusal with no "would have"; 220 outcome alerts for 145 entries.
  - **The fix.** Replay's verdict is chosen before the description: an entry whose index `state.Rejected` lists is reported once, as "the log published entry N, <who> would have <done what> — refused: <reason>. … the entry did not take effect", through `plainlog.DescribeRejected` (the conditional form of `Describe`, which is unchanged); an applied entry is described as before; an undecodable one says its intended action cannot be read. One outcome per served entry, in log order; the six SEC-001 `repeated-entry` alarms stay as the separate Critical alerts they are; `reported` and `rejectedSeen` keep an unchanged log silent — and that test now accepts no alert of any kind on a second round, a tightening worth having.
