The fourteen socket tests the sandbox skipped ran here, green; `go vet ./...` found no other caller of `RejectedEntry`'s old shape. Both of the lane's controls rerun on master (digests checked): the rejected-index branch bypassed fails the never-described-as-done test; the "would have" wording dropped fails the two wording tests.

- **6.5m-sec-008c — `norn govern` exists (Codex lane I, integrated); SEC-008 closes with it.**
  - **What it does.** One command, `norn govern -t TYPE`, for the ten §4.3 governance types — `signer_add/remove/thr`, `root_add/remove/thr`, `log_key`, `policy`, `params`, `note` — signed as a root, extendable by the next root from a file, a positional path or stdin, and submitted with `norn submit`. `-yes` is refused before anything is read: a root's authority is never scripted, so every invocation confirms, and a piped entry takes its confirmation from the terminal rather than from bytes in the pipe. The signing key must be an observed root; the body is checked against the observed state as §5.1 will check it — `dup-key`, `unknown-key`, `root-invariant`, `bad-thr` (D-033), a policy that parses, params typed as §4.5 says — so a root learns why a change is unusable before being asked to approve it, and none of it changes replay (D-046 still counts the quorum before the body). Flags on an extension are constraints, never replacements, and every existing root signature is verified before the summary and again after signing. The summary shows every field — a key by kid and hex, a threshold as "N of M", a policy's quorum line and witnesses, each param — the quorum progress, the guard and the entry hash, free text quoted.
  - **Ten tests** drive the binary with `yes\n` on stdin and replay the output: a three-root `signer_add` applies and one or two roots fail `threshold`; every other type replays to its specified effect (`params` checked through canonical `state.json`, `policy` kept verbatim, `note` changing nothing); twenty-four refusals; `-yes` refused for all ten types; tampered bodies and signatures; flag/body agreement on extension for seven types; foreign and malformed entries over stdin; the summary before the prompt; public and private key files read without being changed; guard choices and `-o` preserved. ENROLLMENT's R1–R3, R7, R8 and §6 now show the invocation.
  - **Integration.** Base `aa87faa`; the tracked changes applied to master cleanly, the README count set from the guard. The seven socket tests the sandbox skipped ran here, green. Five of the lane's sixteen controls rerun on master (digests checked): `-yes` allowed, the root check dropped, the `root-invariant` pre-check dropped, the `bad-thr` pre-check dropped, existing signatures unchecked before the summary — each failing its named test.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1017 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-035-i — preshared keys survive owner mode; `norn status` judges expiry in witness time (Codex lane J, integrated); the overlap refusal split off as 035-ii.**
  - **What it does.** `peertable.Peer` gains an operator-managed `PresharedKey` (zero means none); the owner plan copies each kept peer's key from the table it is replacing, since the log says nothing about preshared keys and a rewrite that dropped one broke a tunnel the operator had hardened; the real backend (`internal/wgdev`, not `internal/peertable` as the brief named it — the lane said so) reads it back and writes it, with a nil pointer meaning "leave it alone", as for an endpoint; the fake keeps it through an endpoint refresh the same way. `norn status` judges expiry at `proven.EvaluationTime` — the witness instant the agent judges at — says which instant it used, and under `quorum none` says it judged nothing rather than guessing. ENFORCEMENT carries one sentence.

The lane proved the fault (both `10.9.0.0/24` and `10.9.0.2/32` are installed today), kept the red test outside the clone, restored `internal/endpoint` exactly, and stopped. That is row 035-ii now, untagged, with the saved test as its red.

Three controls rerun on master (digests checked): the owner carry-over removed, the backend's read removed, `status` on the wall clock again — each failing its named test.

- **6.5m-sec-002m — the monitor compares heads (Codex lane H, integrated); SEC-002's third point and SEC-007's monitor half close.**
  - **What it does.** Each round, every node's verified head is compared with the log's verified head, with that node's own earlier verified view, and with every other node that verified this round — with `tlog.Tree.HeadAt` at the smaller size, the same comparison a node's §10 check makes, over trees that already verified, so no proof from either source is trusted. Two histories are a Critical `conflicting-heads` alert naming both sources, sizes and roots and pointing at `norn verify-evidence`; a node merely behind is not; and a node that goes backwards along its *own* consistent history is a Critical `view-rollback` — the lane's own call on a question the brief left open, and the right one: it is D-069's failure seen from outside. An unverified answer neither compares nor erases a view; the kept view is the greatest size seen, so a shrinking answer cannot hide history. Each conflicting pair is reported once, whatever the poll order.
  - **One seam, for the sandbox and for tests:** `Watcher.NodeFetcher`, defaulting to `gossip.Peer(node.URL)`; the new tests serve node views from `detect/`'s shipped branches through it, with `honest-earlier` as the log where equal sizes matter, and never open a socket.
  - **Eleven tests**; the lane's six controls each failed their named test and were restored. **Integration.** The lane worked from `cbb088d`; its four monitor files applied to master cleanly, its README count was stale and is set from the guard. The fourteen socket tests the sandbox skipped ran here, green. Four controls rerun on master (digests checked): the equal-size comparison skipped fails the same-size test; a prefix mismatch ignored fails the longer-fork test; the previous view not compared fails the changing-history test; the once-per-pair suppression off fails the unchanged-pair test.
  - **A refinement to record, not a defect:** pairs are keyed by head, so a fork that persists while the log keeps growing is a new pair each round — a Critical alert per new log size. If that proves noisy in the lab, key the suppression by source pair; LAB.md §3's cadence rule would then apply.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone — green in all 49 packages with tests once the README count the guard asked for was set (1002 tests) — `vectors-check`, 224 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-008b — `norn rotate` exists (Codex lane G, integrated).**
  - **What it does.** `norn rotate -device ID -wg-key FILE | -wg-pub KEY [-new-key FILE]` signs a §4.3 `rotate` entry as the device — the default role, so `-yes` is allowed, since a device rotates with nobody at the keyboard — or extends one as a signer when `rotate_needs_signer` is on; `norn submit` sends it. With `-new-key` the incoming identity key signs beside the current one on the same preimage (D-032), and the command refuses to let it do anything else: only the current `device_pk` may initiate or extend as the device. It reads a WireGuard private key only to derive the public half, and never generates, writes or prints one — a test watches the directory and the output for both.
  - **What it refuses before any prompt**, none of it a new replay rule: an unknown or revoked device; the pre-rotation key `nas` (the fixture rotated its identity) and a stranger's; a `wg_pk` active for another device (`dup-wg`); a rotation that changes nothing; an incoming key equal to the current; `-new-key` with `-role signer` or when extending; a malformed key; an extension of another type, network or device, with an unknown body field, a disagreeing `-wg-pub`/`-wg-key`, or a signature that does not verify — including one by a root, and one by the device's own key under the wrong role.

  - **Integration.** The lane worked from `cbb088d`; its tracked changes applied to master cleanly, its README count was stale and is set from the guard. The seven socket tests the sandbox skipped ran here, green. Four of the lane's five controls rerun on master (digests checked): the role lookup before signing dropped fails `superseded_device_key` — disabling only the `bytes.Equal` after it proves nothing, as in lane F, because the lookup already binds the stored key's kid to the signing key's, so that line is defence in depth; the incoming key not signing fails the possession test (replay's `no-device-sig`); the `dup-wg` pre-check off fails `duplicate_WG_key`; existing signatures unchecked fails the tampered-entry test. ENROLLMENT §4 shows the device's invocation and the signer's extension.

- **6.5m-sec-dec — one DECISION block for the five protocol questions the audit raised; no 🧠 row remains.**
  - **The block** (above the D-071 block in this file) takes SEC-021, 022, 023, 014 and 033 in turn: what is true on master, the options with what each costs, and a recommendation each — keep a frozen node's hands off the interface but have it name what it is not evicting; make a present-but-empty `labels` map a schema fault; have §3 admit only prime-order keys with canonical encodings and state the verification equation, vectored at the edges; say in R7 that rotation is not revocation and leave retirement to v1.1; have `nornd` refuse to enforce under `quorum none` unless a setting says so. Every recommendation is the first option, and the block says how to answer.
  - **What it unblocks.** Five rows (021r, 022r, 023r, 014r, 033r), each marked with the part it needs, with owners by rule 12: 023r is a protocol row with new vectors and stays Mythos; 022r and 014r are lanes; 021r and 033r are Opus. Nothing else on the track waits on them.

- **6.5m-iv-d — the mirror writes only what changed, durably, checkpoint last; the `publishKey` twins fold into `durable`; H4 closes.**
  - **Red first.** A 300-entry log grown by one rewrote its full bundle, its full tile and its level-1 tile — the same bytes at the same paths — and the mirror's writer was a plain temp-and-rename that synced nothing, so after a power cut its head could name a file the disk never received and D-069's restart reported the mirror unusable (the cost D-069 accepted and this row pays). And `durable` had no exclusive publication: a `Publish` stub that replaced failed both of the twins' tests moved there.
  - **The mirror.** Every file goes through one writer, `durable.WriteFile`, and only when its bytes are not already there; the checkpoint goes last, as before, so a crash leaves a mirror advertising less than it holds. A re-signed head writes the checkpoint and nothing else; a grown head writes the partial bundle, the partial tile and the checkpoint. The writer is a package variable so a test can watch the order; the choice of `durable` behind it is by construction and has no control, said rather than claimed.
  - **The twins.** `durable.Publish` is the exclusive publication both `keyfile` and `wgkey` carried in full (6.5m-sec-025): bytes flushed before the name exists, the name made by an exclusive link so a file that appeared after any earlier check is never replaced, the temporary removed before the directory is flushed, Windows skipping the directory sync. `PublishWith` keeps the sync seam the twins' tests drive. Each twin is now four lines: the call, and its own words on the one error an operator meets. Their tests are unchanged and green; `durable` has its own copies.
  - **Three controls**, each restored byte for byte (digests checked): the byte-equality skip removed fails the grown-log test and the order test; the checkpoint written first fails the order test; the exclusive link replaced by a rename fails `durable`'s never-replaces test (and, through the wrappers, the twins' tests, which is the fold working).
  - **H4 closes** with a–d: a fold that resumes, a verification that costs what grew, an agent that uses it and re-verifies in full on a cadence, and a mirror that keeps up without rewriting its history. Stale partial files (an old `001.p/44` beside the new `001.p/45`) are left in place; a reader fetches the path the size implies, and removing them is a tidiness the row did not name.

- **6.5m-iv-c — the agent verifies from what it holds, and in full on every doubt.**
  - **Red first.** Over an unchanged log the second cycle fetched the checkpoint, the bundle and the tile again; and a tile rewritten after the head was adopted was refused on the very next cycle — which sounds right and is not what H4-b decided: the held head vouched for those bytes, and refusing them every cycle is the full re-verification H4 exists to stop doing.
  - **The rule, in `verifyLog`.** The log is verified **from the held head** when that head was verified in this process (`a.last`), and **in full** otherwise: on a first cycle, when the head was restored from the node's own mirror (D-069: nothing on disk is believed because this node wrote it — the restored head is held and compared against, never resumed from), and every `FullVerifyEvery` (5 min, `DefaultFullVerifyEvery`, H3's figure), which is what catches a bundle or tile rewritten below the held head since. The genesis refusal `verify` adds is shared (`checkGenesis`). Peers are still verified in full: they are asked rarely and their branch is the question.
  - **Four tests.** An unchanged log's second cycle costs the checkpoint alone (H3-a's fifty-cycle form of the same property is left to H3); a restarted node's first cycle fetches everything although it holds a restored head; a tile corrupted after adoption passes the next cycle and is refused at the first full verification, `VERIFY_FAILED` and `ENFORCING_ON_STALE_STATE` once each; a copy of entry 37 appended after the held head is `dup-entry` and the active set unchanged — the seen set travelled with the fold.

H2-c's slow-log test had to grow its log: an unchanged head is one request now, and one request is never over budget.

- **6.5m-iv-b — `logclient.VerifyFrom`: a grown head costs what grew.**
  - **Red first.** With `VerifyFrom` as a stub that called `Verify`, the counting test showed an unchanged 300-entry log costing every bundle and every tile; the property test, which agrees trivially under that stub, instead found the suite served over the wrong log — `served-bad/` is served over `served-large/`, not `served/` — and was restructured per suite.
  - **What it does.** The head checks — the anchor's soundness, the log signature, the origin, the quorum — are one `verifyHead` for both verifiers, and the rest of §10 one `finish`. `VerifyFrom` fetches the bundles from the one the held size falls in (none when the size has not grown), requires the entries below the held size in a refetched bundle to be the held ones, appends the rest to a **copy** of the held tree (`tlog.Tree.Clone`), and requires the served head to be that tree's head — which is the held→new consistency check, with no proof from anyone. It checks only the tiles whose path (width included) is not among the held tree's, and resumes a **copy** of the held fold (`replay.Replayer.Clone`, over a new `state.Clone`), so a verification that fails halfway leaves what the node holds untouched. Where the cheap path cannot decide — a size below the held one, a refetched bundle that differs below the held size, a head that is not the held tree extended — it hands the whole question to `Verify`, so the answer is `Verify`'s, code for code, fork included. `Result` carries its fold, unexported.
  - **The property, and what it honestly says.** For every held size sampled (the ends, the middle, the tile edges, and each `detect/` stored size) and every case of the three suites, the two verifiers are compared. A case's defect is *visible* when a path it changes — found by diffing its directory against the honest log, not by reading `cases.json` — is one `VerifyFrom` fetches at that held size; on those the two agree code for code and, when both accept, verify the same head and replay to the same bytes. Where the defect lies below the held head `VerifyFrom` accepts and `Verify` refuses, by design: the held head vouched for those bytes when it was adopted, and a tile or bundle rewritten since is for H3's periodic full verification. `detect/tampered-bundle-under-a-stored-head` at the full held size is exactly that case, and the test names the trade rather than hiding it.
  - **Counting.** A 300-entry log grown by one entry costs the checkpoint, the partial bundle it landed in and the partial tile that changed — three fetches, named exactly; bundle 0, tile 0/000 and the level-1 tile are not asked for. The same log unchanged costs the checkpoint alone.
  - **Three controls**, each restored byte for byte (digests checked): the bundle loop started one bundle late fails the counting test; the held-entries comparison skipped fails the rewritten-entry test; the head-mismatch handover to `Verify` removed fails the property. The first two proved nothing on the first run, and the reasons shaped the tests: a 146-entry log has one bundle and one tile, so a late offset falls back to `Verify` and fetches *exactly the expected set* — the counting test now grows a 300-entry log this package signs itself, where a fallback would refetch the full bundle 0; and the suite's tampered entries sit at indexes that are always fresh at the sampled held sizes, so a new test rewrites entry 256 inside the refetched partial bundle under the honest checkpoint, where only that comparison stands between `VerifyFrom` and a wrong acceptance.

- **6.5m-sec-004r-c — a first head is corroborated before it is trusted for long; row 004r closes.**
  - **Red first, three ways.** A fresh owner node whose log serves a branch (`forkedLog` at 40) and whose one peer holds the real log: the branch was enforced and the peer not asked — "a first head contradicted by a peer was accepted". A fresh node whose peer is unreachable: enforced, silent, and a cycle later, with the peer up on the other branch, nothing happened until `T_g`. A fresh node whose peer agrees: asked zero times in its first cycle.
  - **The rule (D-071 c), in `Once`.** With no held head — `a.last` and `a.restored` both nil — and peers configured, the first verified head is **uncorroborated**: peers are asked in the same cycle with that head as §10's stored checkpoint, before anything is enforced, and in every cycle after until one answers. A peer's head that verifies (equal, or extending — then adopted, said as a corroboration rather than a stale-log rescue) clears the flag; one on another branch is a fork proven with the table untouched, and the evidence is filed against the first head, which `recordFork` now takes explicitly because nothing is held yet. No peer answering: the head is enforced, `FIRST_HEAD_UNCORROBORATED` once (WARN in `nornd`), and the asking continues. A fork proven against a head this node enforced uncorroborated: `apply(nil)` — `reconcile` is now a choice of set plus `apply`, the same path `hard_stale` takes — then the freeze; the FORK alarm says the peers were dropped rather than that the table is unchanged. A peer merely behind does not corroborate (it vouches only for the prefix) and the asking continues; a node with no peers configured corroborates with nobody, as D-071 says.

Those peers verified under the anchor when the node last ran, and `nornd` already wires `Peers` to this function, so a rebooted node's first cycle can now ask them. The restored head is still only held: the same test checks that nothing was installed.

- **6.5m-sec-004r-a — the witness clock survives a restart; `S_hard` is no longer a limit a restart lifts.**
  - **Red first, and the line that matters:** a node on the fixture log, two hours on the same head, is `degraded` (and `hard_stale` with `S_hard` = 1 h, its table emptied). A second agent over the same state directory, monotonic clock at zero, the log serving the very same head: `fresh`, no alarm, and "a restart reopened 6 peers an S_hard drop had closed" — audit SEC-004's open point 1, reproduced.
  - **The fix (D-071 a), in `clock.go`.** `saveClock` writes the clock's estimate of now — the newest quorum time seen, carried forward by monotonic time — to `<state_dir>/clock` (`norn-clock/v1`, Unix seconds) with `durable.WriteFile`, once it has advanced a minute past the last write, whatever the log is doing: the write runs on the ordinary path and on the no-state-yet path, because an outage is exactly when the file matters. `restoreClock`, called from `New` beside `restoreHead`, seeds the clock from it as an instant observed now — a lower bound on now, so a head's age after the restart is at least what it was at the last write. A file that does not parse is `CLOCK_UNUSABLE` and ignored; a missing one is a first start and silent. The head's own quorum time is still never the seed (H1's argument stands: it says when witnesses signed, not how long the node has watched).
  - **Three tests** in `clock_test.go`: the restart keeps `degraded` and `hard_stale` (and the table stays empty under `S_hard`); the file is written at the first head, not rewritten at 30 s, and advances by two hours with the log gone; a garbage file is reported once and the node starts with no clock. `nornd` reports the new kind at WARN.

- **6.5m-sec-008a — `norn revoke` exists; the runbooks' first step is a command now (Codex lane F, integrated).**
  - **What it does.** `norn revoke -device ID [-reason TEXT]` signs a §4.3 revoke entry as a signer, a root, or the device itself (`-role`), or extends one another signer started (`-in FILE`, a positional file, or `-` for stdin); `norn submit` sends the finished entry, as for `sign`. It reuses `sign`'s anchor loading, signer opening, observed-size guard, confirmation and output, and changes neither `sign.go` nor `submit.go`.
  - **What it refuses, before any prompt.** `-yes` with `-role root`; a device that is unknown or not active in the verified log; a key that is not the claimed role's (a device's key must be its *current* `device_pk`, so the pre-rotation key is refused); a reason over 256 bytes; an entry to extend that is another type, another network, carries an unknown body field, names another device or a different reason, or carries a signature that does not verify over it. It verifies every signature again after signing, so adding one can neither bless a tampered input nor break an earlier approval. A verified log is required even with `-after` or `-no-after`: those choose the guard, but cannot show that the device is active or the key holds the role.
  - **Tests drive the binary against the vector log.** Eight tests: signer quorum (one signature fails threshold, two revoke), self-revocation with the rotated key, an interactive three-root quorum, fifteen refusals, seven mismatched extensions, the summary before the prompt, guard choices kept through extension, a tampered entry refused. Each replays the result against the fixture and checks `nas` is revoked and gone from `active_wg`.

A fifth, written here first, disabled only the `bytes.Equal` after the lookup and proved nothing — the lookup already binds the stored key's `kid` to the signing key's, so that line only matters on a 64-bit `kid` collision; it stays as defence in depth.

The seven socket tests the sandbox had to skip ran here, green. ENROLLMENT §4 shows the invocation and the extend-and-submit flow; `rotate` stays planned (008b).

- **6.5m-sec-001b — SEC-001 fixed in the protocol (D-070); 010-ii's vector rides along; rows 001b and 010 close.**
  - **The rule, in both implementations.** §5.1 step 1's duplicate key is now the entry's **signed content** — SHA-256 of the signature preimage — when the entry decodes and its envelope passes §4.1, `net` included, and its bytes otherwise. The same content under any other signature list is the same entry, so a copy of a past entry with one unresolvable signature added, a surplus one dropped or a role relabelled is `dup-entry` at step 1, before any later rule can judge it, whatever the original's own outcome was. An entry that does not decode keeps its byte key, so the existing undecodable-copy vectors still read `dup-entry`. Both sides compute the key the same way on purpose: Go's `entry.Decode` plus the `net` comparison, the reference's `cbor.decode` plus `_check_envelope`, so a wrong-network copy falls to the byte key on both.
  - **Red first, both sides.** Copies of `37-enroll-spare`, `28-policy`, `35-rotate-nas`, `16-signer_add-signer3` and `89-two-sig-base` under each variant: four were **accepted** outright (the last rejection was the fixture's own tail), the rest were refused by a later rule — `threshold`, `no-device-sig` — rather than as duplicates. After: every one `dup-entry`, `spare` stays revoked, the policy and the signer set stay. A different content under the same signatures is not a duplicate.
  - **The log grows once, 138 → 145.** Six `bad-copy-*` entries, one per variant and scenario, and 010-ii's `bad-params-mixed-validity` (`mmd` valid, `staleness` a bool; `state.json` shows `mmd` unchanged by it). `two-sig-base` carries its own text now — under D-070 its old content was `profile-base`'s, and a control that is itself `dup-entry` controls nothing — so the sigs-ordering negative keeps a live control instead of 89 flipping, which the decision had predicted. Served, proofs and `SHA256SUMS` regenerated; `anchors/` restamped with the pinned `python-opentimestamps` over the new checkpoint (`checkpoint-145.ots`); the entries after the insertion renumbered by seven, and every spec citation, the §6 tile examples, the rejecting-entry count (95 → 102) and one guard's pinned name followed.
  - **The spec.** §4.0 gains `content_hash` beside `entry_hash`, whose row now says what it is the identity of; the two passages that argued for a byte key — the shortest-form rule and the whole-input rule — are re-argued under D-070 (both rules stay load-bearing: they are what makes a second encoding `decode` rather than a question for the duplicate check); §5.1 step 1 and the genesis's step 1 say the key; §5.2's row names it; §12.1's seen-set row names the six vectors and the `params` row the seventh. D-031's heading points at D-070. README's and `THREAT-MODEL.md`'s "open defect SEC-001" notes are gone, and A2 says the copy is a duplicate.
  - **Three of this session's own tests had to move**: they built a junk-signed copy of entry 37 exactly as the fixture's new entry 114 does, so the log server saw an exact resubmission and the monitor an exact repeat. They use a different junk `kid` now, and the monitor's first-round test expects the six fixture copies, each naming its original.

- **6.5m-sec-011-ii — `Open` refuses to start below the checkpoint it last signed; 6.5m-sec-011 closes.**
  - **The damage a reader cannot resolve.** After 011-i, recovery reads past whatever a crash left in a partial directory. But bundles can be lost as well as torn — a disk error, a bad restore — and a store that recovers fewer entries than the checkpoint it last signed and published would sign and publish a smaller head: a log that shrank, which every node refuses as a rollback and a self-witnessed log proves as a fork against itself. Red first: a five-entry store with its partial directory deleted opened at size zero.
  - **The rule.** `Open` reads the size the on-disk checkpoint claims — its signature unchecked, since it was this store's own and a forged larger number can only make a store refuse to open — and refuses when the bundles recover fewer entries, naming both sizes and telling the operator to restore the bundles. A checkpoint *behind* the bundles is the designed crash (it is written last) and a torn one is the same case: both open at the bundles' size and republish, and two tests pin that.
  - **Two controls**, each alone and restored byte for byte: the comparison removed fails the refusal test; the comparison inverted fails it and the behind case.
  - **011 closes:** a new partial is written and synced before the old is removed, temporaries and lying names are ignored, the directory is synced, and `Open` refuses to start below its last checkpoint. The package comment's "behind what is on disk, never ahead" is true again, and `PLAN.md`'s clean-restart line now has a crash behind it.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone, green in all 49 packages with tests — 943 tests — `vectors-check`, 222 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-011-i — the log store's recovery reads what is there, not what a crash left (SEC-011, first of two).**
  - **The probe, now a test.** A 5-entry log with one empty `.tmp-*` left in its partial-bundle directory — what a power cut between creating and writing a temporary leaves — reopened at **size 0**. `readBundle` globbed the directory, took the first match, and an empty file decodes to no entries; `recover` then stopped at the last full bundle, which for any log under 256 entries is the genesis boundary. The store signed and published that head.
  - **Three things a crash can leave, three rules.** A temporary is never a bundle: dot-prefixed names are skipped, and a name that is not a width in range is too. Two widths side by side mean the crash fell between writing the new partial and removing the old, and the log is the wider one. A name is only a claim: a file counts only if it decodes to exactly the width its name gives, so a torn copy or a lying name is passed over for the next; a directory that holds candidates and no readable bundle is an error, not a shorter log. And the write order is now the safe one — the new partial is written, synced and renamed before older widths are removed, and the directory is synced after each rename (skipped on Windows, as `internal/durable` does) — so what a crash leaves is at worst two widths, which the reader resolves.
  - **Tests, red first:** the leftover temporary (0 → 5); two widths (4 and 5 → 5); a file named `9` holding four entries beside the real `5` (→ 5).
  - **Three controls**, each alone and restored byte for byte: the old first-match read restored, verbatim, fails the first two; the widths in ascending order fails the second; the name's width unchecked fails the third. The write-then-remove order and the directory sync are not observable by a test on a working disk — recorded as reviewed, not proven, like `durable`'s sync.
  - **Still open in this row:** `Open` refusing to start below the checkpoint it last signed (ii), for the damage a reader cannot resolve.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone, green in all 49 packages with tests — 941 tests — `vectors-check`, 222 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-010-i — a rejected `params` entry changes nothing, in either implementation.**
  - **The bug, now a test in each implementation.** §5.1 says a rejected entry changes nothing. Both `params` handlers wrote each key as they validated it, so an entry with one good key and one bad — `{mmd: 60, staleness: true}`, root-signed — was rejected `decode` after `mmd` had already landed. In the reference that happened deterministically (canonical key order puts `mmd` first); in Go it depended on map order, so two nodes replaying one log disagreed on `mmd`, and one node disagreed with itself from poll to poll. The triage probe measured 31 flips in 200 replays; the Go test, which replays 200 times and requires every one rejected and `params` untouched, went red on its third replay.
  - **The fix** is the same in both: validate every key into a temporary map, apply only when all pass. No protocol change: the rule was already §5.1's; the implementations were wrong.
  - **Two controls**, each alone and restored byte for byte: Go writing as it goes fails the Go test; the reference writing as it goes fails the reference test.

- **6.5m-sec-029 — a log for another genesis never empties the peer table.**
  - **The hole, from the triage probe.** Replay aborts on an entry 0 that is not the pinned genesis and returns an empty state with `bad-genesis` at index 0; `logclient.Verify` returned that as a success. A node given a trust file for another network, or a corrupted one, and served this log, then verified it — correctly signed, cosigned, replayed to nothing — and in owner mode installed the empty set: six peers to none, no error, no alarm. The audit rated this low; it breaks the agent's first promise, that a failure never widens or empties the table.
  - **The fix is at the node, not yet the verifier.** `agent.verify` wraps `logclient.Verify` for every path a node verifies through — the log, a peer, the mirror at restart — and refuses a result whose checkpoint has entries but whose state has none: such a log is not this network's, and nothing in it is a fact about this network. The refusal is reported as a failed verification (`VERIFY_FAILED`, then `NO_STATE_YET` or `ENFORCING_ON_STALE_STATE` as usual) and the table stays. It carries no §10.1 code: a code for a served log whose entry 0 is not the genesis is run 13's D12, a protocol question for 6.5l-ix, and `norn verify`'s own answer waits on it.
  - **Tests, red first:** owner and watchdog modes over a six-peer table and the shipped log under a wrong genesis — error, table unchanged, `VERIFY_FAILED` and `NO_STATE_YET`; and a peer serving that log while the node's own log is dead — refused, not adopted.
  - **Three controls**, each alone and restored byte for byte: the refusal removed fails all three cases; the peer path bypassing the wrapper fails the peer test; the direct path bypassing it fails both modes. The mirror path shares the wrapper and has no test of its own: a node never mirrors what it refused, so the case needs a trust file changed under an existing mirror, which the unusable-mirror tests of H1-b cover for the origin and not yet for the genesis.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone, green in all 49 packages with tests — 937 tests — `vectors-check`, 221 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-005a-iii — `loadFreeze` checks what it loads and fails closed; 6.5m-sec-005a closes.**
  - **What a freeze file found at start is.** It was written by this node when it had proof, or it is a marker left when the proof could not be filed. Until now `loadFreeze` honoured any evidence file for this origin without reading past its header. It now checks the evidence as a stranger would, under the trust file — and **the freeze holds either way**. The usual reason a genuine file stops verifying is a rotated trust file for the same network (SEC-005 b; the R7 runbook), and that is not §11's reset, which is a new trust file for a different origin. A file that would not convince anybody else is something the operator must know before carrying it to the witness operators, not a reason to start enforcing again.
  - **The alarm says which.** `FROZEN_BY_FORK` now carries a note: for evidence that does not verify, the refusal and "the freeze stands"; for a marker, "a marker, not evidence" and the reason it was written; for verifying evidence, nothing — it is reported as proof, plainly. The in-process marker paths set the same note.
  - **Tests, red first on the alarm:** a rotated trust file over a real evidence file keeps the node frozen and the alarm says the file does not verify; a marker's reason reaches the alarm; verifying evidence carries no doubt.
  - **Five controls**, each alone and restored byte for byte: unverifiable evidence unfreezing the node; no note when the check fails; doubt attached when the check passes; the marker's reason not loaded; the note not carried by the alarm.
  - **005a closes**: a node shown the longer branch writes evidence (i), a freeze is persisted even when evidence cannot be built (ii), and `loadFreeze` checks what it loads (iii) — each red first from the triage probe or the rotation scenario. What remains of SEC-005 is (b) and (c), row 005bc: evidence checked under learned keys and the replayed policy, which will also make (ii)'s rotation scenario build real evidence again.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone, green in all 49 packages with tests — 935 tests — `vectors-check`, 221 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-005a-ii — a freeze marker when the evidence cannot be built (SEC-005 a, second of three).**
  - **Why the freeze cannot depend on the file.** §11 says a forked node refuses everything inconsistent with its view *forever*, and 4.6b made that outlive a process by making the evidence file the freeze. After 005a-i the evidence can still fail to be built in a way a real deployment produces: a node that followed a log-key rotation (D-020) holds a head signed by a key its trust file does not name, so the self-check it runs on its own evidence — under the trust file's key — refuses it (SEC-005 b, row 005bc). The node then raised FORK, froze in memory only, and a restart unfroze it. Red first on exactly that scenario.
  - **The marker.** When evidence cannot be filed, by this node or from a peer, the node writes `fork/<unix>.frozen`: a magic line, this network's origin, and the reason, through the same durable, never-overwriting filing as evidence. `loadFreeze` reads evidence first, then markers, and a marker for this origin freezes the node; one for another origin is ignored, so §11's reset by a new trust file still works. A marker proves nothing to anybody else, so gossip never serves it; the FORK alarm names it and the reason.
  - **Tests:** the rotation scenario, which skips itself if evidence turns out to be buildable (after 005bc lands it will, and the marker path keeps the unit test below); and a round-trip — a marker written for this network freezes the next start, one for another network does not.
  - **Three controls**, each alone and restored byte for byte: no marker written on failure; markers not loaded; a marker honoured for any network.
  - **Still open in this row:** `loadFreeze` checking what it loads while failing closed (iii).
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone, green in all 49 packages with tests — 932 tests — `vectors-check`, 221 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-005a-i — evidence when the served branch is the longer one (SEC-005 a, first of three).**
  - **The hole, from the triage probe, now a test.** The verifier detects a fork at the smaller of the two sizes, in either direction (6.5l-vii-d-ii). But evidence was built only one way — this node's own tree speaking for the conflicting head's size — and a node holding the shorter branch has no root at that size. So a log that forked and then grew past this node's head raised FORK, built nothing ("this node cannot speak for size 138"), froze in memory only, and a restart unfroze it. Growing past the victim is the natural shape of a forking log. The unmerged branch fixed this on 2026-09-30 (`bdb3086`); master never got it, and its diff was read as evidence while this was built here.
  - **The fix.** §11.1's `held` is "the branch the accuser can speak for, because it has the entries". When the served branch is the longer one, the node has just fetched every served entry, so that is the branch it can speak for: the served head becomes `held`, the stored head `conflicting`, and `size` is the stored size. `writeEvidence` swaps the roles exactly then. The reader's four checks are unchanged — `size` is at or below `held`'s size, the proof chains the served tree from the stored size to its head, and the roots differ — so this clarifies the accuser's side of §11.1 and changes nothing a reader accepts or refuses; the `held` row says it in one sentence.
  - **The test** holds a 16-entry forked branch, is served the real 138-entry log, and requires: a `ForkError`; one evidence file; that file **verifying under the trust file** with the fork at size 16; and a restart that comes back frozen. Red first, on the probe's exact error.
  - **Two controls**, each alone and restored byte for byte: the swap removed fails the new test; the swap the wrong way round fails it and the existing shorter-branch test too, so both directions are pinned by one line.
  - **Still open in this row:** a freeze marker when evidence cannot be built at all (ii), and `loadFreeze` checking what it loads while failing closed (iii).
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone, green in all 49 packages with tests — 930 tests — `vectors-check`, 221 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-001a — SEC-001's outside route is closed at the log's door, and its use is seen by the monitor; D-070 taken.**
  - **The decision, first.** The owner chose option A, recorded as D-070: `dup-entry` is keyed on the signed content for every entry, accepted or rejected; per-device sequence numbers (option E) are recorded for v1.1; C is a strict subset of A. The protocol change itself is 001b. This row is what needs no decision and protects a deployment today.
  - **`norn-log` refuses a re-signed copy.** `add` already returned the receipt for an exact resubmission, by entry hash. Now, right after that, a submission whose signature preimage (§4.2, the envelope without `sigs`) matches any stored entry that decodes is refused 409, naming the index that already holds that content and citing D-070. The courtesy replay stays as it was. Red: a copy of `37-enroll-spare` with one unresolvable signature was answered 200 with a receipt — the exact attack, accepted. Exact resubmission is still idempotent.

The watcher remembers the hash of every reported entry's preimage, and the hash of its bytes, across rounds. Only a copy with the same content and **different bytes** is reported: the first implementation flagged entries 13, 85 and 113 too, which are exact repeats that every verifier refuses as `dup-entry` and the rejected-entry rule already reports. The shipped log's 70/89 pair is reported once on a first round and not again on an unchanged log.

A test was added where a copy of entry 37 lands after the monitor has watched the whole log, built on a writable, cosigned copy of the fixture (`fixtureLog`), and the control now fails it.

- **6.5m-sec-009 — a cosignature is attributed to the witness whose key verified it (Codex lane E).**
  - **What was wrong.** `cosign.Verify` matches a line on the witness's note name and key id, as §10 requires, and returns the key that verified it. But the four places that evaluate the quorum — the verifier, proof bundles, fork evidence and the witness clock — mapped each cosignature to a policy label by note name alone, through `Policy.Label`, which returns the first witness whose key carries that name. Two keys sharing a note name are legal under C2SP (and stay so: the parser refuses duplicate public keys and duplicate short names, not duplicate note names). The lane's red output shows both halves: under a flat `group g 2 a b` where a and b share a name, a valid a+b was refused as `[a a]` — fail-closed — and under `quorum a`, b alone was **accepted** as a. A party counted as another.
  - **What lane E built** (`gpt-6.1-sol`, reasoning high). `Policy.LabelFor(noteName, public)` returns the short name of the witness whose verifier key has that name **and** that public key, or nothing. All four callers use it and drop a cosignature no witness line matches, rather than mislabel it; in the witness clock that also means a line from a key the policy does not carry contributes no time. `Label` stays for one specdoc helper that deliberately attributes blindly. Tests at each caller: a+b satisfies 2-of-2, b alone does not, b cannot stand for a, a meets its own quorum; and the clock's two cases. No vector: the suite is generated, and a shipped case for two witnesses sharing a note name is noted for the next log regeneration (6.5m-sec-010 grows the log).
  - **Reviewed here, with one merge.** Every line read. Lane E was cloned before lane C landed and both appended to the end of the policy files, so the two hunks were merged three-way here, keeping both; two closing braces lost at the seam were restored and the package is green. The lane's five controls rerun with byte-verified restores — `LabelFor` ignoring the key, and each of the four callers back to name-only — each fails its test. The lane could not run `internal/logclient`'s four HTTP tests in its sandbox and said so; they ran here under race, green.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone, green in all 49 packages with tests — 925 tests — `vectors-check`, 221 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-002 — the witness collusion bound stated right, warned about at `norn init`, and guarded (Codex lane C).**
  - **What was wrong.** README G2 and `THREAT-MODEL.md` A9 and G2 said a fork needs "fewer than k witnesses colluding with the log". Two k-of-N quorums share at least 2k−N witnesses, so the log needs only max(0, 2k−N) colluders: it shows each honest witness one consistent branch, and the colluders sign both. Under the shipped 2-of-3 policy that is **one** witness. With 2k ≤ N it is none, and the quorum alone proves nothing about a fork — detection then rests on checkpoint gossip between nodes (6.5l-vii-d-xii-ii, T1).
  - **What lane C built** (`gpt-6.1-sol`, reasoning high). `Policy.CollusionBound` returns max(0, 2k−N) for a flat single-group quorum, counting the group's members rather than every declared witness, and declines (`ok = false`) for `quorum none`, a single-witness quorum and a nested policy, whose overlaps a single k and N cannot describe. `norn init` prints the bound whenever k < N and a warning when it is zero; informational, never a refusal. A `docclaims` guard requires the corrected statement in all three places and refuses the old one even beside a correct formula, with a test that the guard itself cannot be relaxed. Tests cover 2-of-3 (1), 3-of-3 (3), 1-of-2 (0), 2-of-4 (0), an unused witness, the nested fixture policy, and the ceremony's output.
  - **Three corrections here.** The lane had collapsed A9's three-case table into one sentence, losing the liveness case and the out-of-scope mitigation; it is a table again, with the bound in the collusion row and the `norn init` warning named. README's G2 cell and the threat model's are tightened and say "one, under 2-of-3". The operator message read "= 1 witnesses colluding"; it now says "= 1 -- that many witnesses colluding with the log can get two histories cosigned".
  - **Reviewed here.** Every line read. The lane's ten controls rerun against the corrected text with byte-verified restores — the bound off by one, a nested or group-less quorum accepted, the warning on 3-of-3, the warning and the note removed, the guard relaxed, each of the three documents reverted — each fails its test. The three packages are green under race.
  - **Gate:** generators first (no change under `testdata/`), then `make test` (race) alone, green in all 49 packages with tests — 919 tests — `vectors-check`, 221 reference tests, `lint`, `fmt-check`, `vet` clean.

- **6.5m-sec-018 — the endpoint provider reads the `ip` label (Codex lane D).**

The fixture, `norn enroll` and the reference write `ip`. The labels provider read `allowed_ips`, a key nothing writes, so a device enrolled as documented was installed with no route — fail closed, and silent.

Neither the bytes nor the directory entry were ever synced.

The publishing step is one function in each package: write the temporary, sync it, `os.Link` it to the final name — which fails if the name exists — remove the temporary, sync the directory. The operator's "already exists; remove it deliberately" error survives, mode stays 0600, and a sync seam lets the tests observe that the bytes reach the disk before the name does and the name before the directory is flushed.

Windows cannot open a directory for writing, `nornd` writes device keys there too (D-055), and `internal/durable` already skips that step on Windows for the same reason — so both functions now do the same, and both tests expect one sync call there instead of two. Vetted for Windows. The two functions are identical twins across the packages; folding them into `internal/durable` is noted for H4-f, where the mirror's writes are rebuilt, rather than refactored here (rule 9).

- **6.5m-sec-021 — every event kind has a deliberate log level; the first Codex lane is integrated, and the lane protocol learns two things.**
  - **What lane B built** (`gpt-6.1-sol`, reasoning high). `nornd`'s `report` warned for eight kinds and logged every other event at Info — a proven fork, a frozen node, every peer dropped as `hard_stale`, a `degraded` view, an unusable mirror. Now the same evidence filed again is the same file, and anything else under that second keeps its name while the new piece takes the next free second. The names stay unix seconds, so they still sort in the order they were filed, which is how gossip picks the newest. Both agent tests were red against the committed code.

Any other refusal gets no second attempt. `logclient.Published` reads that state **without** verifying the head; its comment says nothing it returns may be held or enforced, and only `Verify` decides. `anchorFor` is now `anchorUnder(state)` plus the held head, so the cycle and the restore build an anchor the same way.
